# Standard QR Decoder

This is the design record for the Standard QR decoder (`QRCodeDecoder`): what it does, why it is scoped this way, and what implementing it taught. Implementation details are in code comments (see the [spec-to-code map](standardqr-spec-map.md)). Micro QR and rMQR have their own records, [Micro QR Decoder](microqr-decoder.md) and [rMQR Decoder](rmqr-decoder.md), and what the three share is in [QR Symbology Architecture](qrcode-symbologies.md).

---

## What

`QRCodeDecoder` decodes QR codes back into text at two levels.

### Matrix level

The input is `QRCodeData` or a byte-per-module span, the format `QRCodeGenerator.Create(Span<byte>)` produces.

The decoder runs the inverse pipeline: format info → unmask → codeword extraction → deinterleave → Reed-Solomon correction → bit stream parsing. The `Span<char>` overloads allocate nothing in steady state.

### Image level

The input is `SKBitmap` or a grayscale luminance span.

Before the matrix pipeline come binarization, finder pattern detection, orientation resolution, bottom-right alignment search (version 2+) and projective grid sampling (4-point perspective transform). Binarization is Otsu, plus a regional pass, in either polarity, when the global threshold reads nothing and gives no verdict on the content. The [spec-to-code map](standardqr-spec-map.md#image-level) draws the stages in order.

The alignment pattern is searched for where the finders' frame puts it, along the frame's grid axes there. That frame is the projective map fixed by the three finder centres and the module sizes at both ends of the two finder lines: a flat symbol in perspective foreshortens along each line, so one plane fits the centres and both size changes. A finder is a candidate when every cross-check line reads 1:1:3:1:1 on its own scale, so a finder drawn up to twice as tall as wide by strong perspective is still found. Where the frame foreshortens, each finder line's module count uses the geometric mean of its two end sizes, the count the frame implies. A cross-check line whose dark runs are all longer or all shorter than their modules (ink spread, a thin print, a blurred ring) is read by the distances between same-polarity edges, and its finder must then also read along its rising diagonal.

If the triple, decoded from the corner its shape names, neither reads nor gives a verdict on the content, each other corner is decoded once its timing patterns read. If the triple still gives neither and more than three candidates were found, up to two other triples are decoded once each, ranked by the height in modules over which their least confirmed finder was confirmed, each from the first of its corners (the shape's included) whose timing patterns read through its own frame.

When nothing anchors the fourth corner (version 1, or no alignment pattern found), the global grid is the parallelogram of the finder centres, followed by the finders' frame when the frame foreshortens. The timing match reads the timing patterns through the frame. Version 14+ also builds a piecewise-bilinear mesh over the full alignment-pattern lattice (wavefront detection with iterated homography refinement), and versions 7-13 build one over their 3 × 3 lattice, searching the four interior nodes where the finders' frame puts them and placing the rest by a least-squares plane. A partially detected mesh falls back to the global transform, so the mesh never decodes worse than that transform.

If a global transform anchored on the bottom-right alignment pattern fails, the decoder falls back to the parallelogram of the three finder centres, which are resolved much more finely at low density. On a grey-level image it is also read by coverage. The resample is decoded only when it samples different modules, and not at the runner-up dimension, which is a guess.

When the estimated dimension fails, the two timing patterns are counted (their dark runs give the version directly), and a version 7+ symbol's version information is read from that sampling. The dimensions these name are tried in that order, then the timing match's, then the estimate's runner-up. An estimate past the version range is not treated as proof of a wrong finder triple: the timing patterns are counted instead, and a count both lines agree on is sampled, or else the timing match's.

On success the result carries the symbol's four corners in image coordinates (`QRCodeDecodeInfo.Corners`, contract in [qrcode-symbologies.md](qrcode-symbologies.md#public-api-direction)) from the mapping that decoded, which on the global path is the 4-point transform. The mesh path runs from version 7 when nothing anchored the fourth corner or the anchored grid did not read, so its corners come from a transform anchored on the three finder centres and the mesh's diagonal-last lattice node (at its last grid coordinate). That node is normally a detected alignment pattern. When the pattern was missed, it is a refinement-round prediction from version 14 and the least-squares plane's placement at versions 7 to 13. Anchoring on the nearest node the mesh detected (tried from version 14) gave byte-identical corners on every version and tilt measured, the erased pattern included, so the simpler form ships. Bilinear extrapolation of the outer mesh cell, tried first, left the top-left corner 0.6 to 0.75 module short, because the finder side of the mesh is only as straight as its first alignment row.

Version 1 has no alignment pattern. Under perspective, whenever the parallelogram grid decodes, its bottom-right corner is the parallelogram estimate the sampler also uses, and error correction lets that grid decode under a few percent of keystone. So the corner tests check a version-2+ keystone to half a module but version 1 only flat and rotated (v1 measured within 0.18 module over a full rotation sweep, so its gap is keystone alone). Past that keystone the parallelogram fails and the finders' frame decodes, so the corners are the frame's (within half a module on the keystoned version 1 renders of `KeystoneFrameDecodeTest`).

The parallelogram fallback is not limited to version 1. `BuildGridTransform` reaches it on any version once all three `allowance` windows miss the bottom-right alignment pattern, and a review round measured that one erased module there is enough. The symbol still decodes through error correction but reports that corner up to about a module and a half out (v2 at 2 % keystone: 0.82 module in either direction. It used to read a little further in one keystone direction only, see the pixel-convention lesson). From version 7 the rest of the alignment lattice anchors the mesh first and the corners come from it: the v10 at 0.75 % that measured 0.83 module off through the parallelogram reports 0.07 through the mesh in either direction (`SymbolCornersTest` checks it to half a module).

The corners are also accurate to half a module only from about 8 px/module up, because the alignment centre is resolved to a whole pixel: its error stays near 4 px at 6, 8 and 12 px/module (4.09, 3.63, 3.94), 0.68 module at the coarse end and 0.33 at the fine one. Both facts are in the public contract. On a grey-level image the alignment centre is now refined to a fraction of a pixel (the centroid lesson below), and these corner figures were not measured again. On a two-level image it is still resolved to a whole pixel.

### Image decode figures

These figures show how the image decoder reads each kind of input. [decode_figures.cs](../../../tools/decode_figures.cs) draws them from the library's own symbols and decodes every rendered input through the public API, so every figure shows a real read. Rerun it when the pipeline changes.

#### Stage by stage

This figure shows a clean symbol on the main path.

![Stage by stage: luminance, global threshold, finder triple, corner from the triangle, alignment search, matrix decode](../images/standardqr/decode-overview.svg)

- Luminance: a grey image comes in.
- Global threshold: one Otsu split of the histogram separates ink from paper.
- Finder triple: each finder reads 1:1:3:1:1 along a line through its centre.
- Corner from the triangle: the top-left finder is the one opposite the longest side.
- Alignment search: the pattern is searched for where the finders' frame predicts it and anchors the four-point transform that samples the grid.
- Matrix decode: format information, unmasking, deinterleaving and Reed-Solomon give the text.

#### Reading the input figures

Each figure shows the input, with the decoder's findings drawn over it, beside its path through the [image-level stages](standardqr-spec-map.md#image-level). Every binarization pass runs this path: the global threshold, then the inverted image, then the regional pass (see [image decode passes](qrcode-symbologies.md#image-decode-passes)). The matrix decode at the bottom reads every grid, and reads it again transposed unless the first read decodes it or gives a verdict on the content.

Green and grey boxes run for this input. Green marks the stages it depends on.

- Key (green): without this stage the input would not read, or would read only after more grids fail than with it. A grid is one sampling of the symbol. Reading it again transposed or by coverage is the same grid.
- Runs (grey): the stage runs as it does for any input.
- Only if needed (dashed): the stage runs only when the grids before it fail.
- Skipped (faded): the stage does not run for this input.

Numbers on the boxes match the numbered notes under each figure.

#### Clean

The input is a screenshot, a render or a flat scan: upright, crisp and flat. The first grid decodes.

![Clean input and its path through the pipeline](../images/standardqr/decode-input-clean.svg)

With only two grey levels, one global threshold splits ink from paper and the grey-level stages stay off. The strided row scan crosses each finder's centre band, and the column, the row again and the falling diagonal confirm each candidate. The top-left finder is opposite the longest side, and the cross product tells the other two apart. In whole pixels the module sizes agree at both ends of each finder line, so the finders' frame is the parallelogram of the centres. The alignment pattern is found where the frame predicts it and anchors the fourth corner.

#### Rotated or mirrored

The symbol is at any angle, mirrored or not.

![Rotated and mirrored input and its path through the pipeline](../images/standardqr/decode-input-rotated.svg)

1. Finder centres and module sizes: sizes are measured along the finder lines, because an image row crosses a turned finder on the slant and reads it up to √2 too long.
2. Matrix decode: a mirrored capture has the same finders but a transposed grid, so a grid that neither reads nor gives a verdict on the content is decoded again, transposed.

A finder reads 1:1:3:1:1 along any line through its centre, so the row scan finds it at any angle. The longest side of the centres' triangle is still the diagonal, so the corner does not depend on the angle. The transform includes the turn, so sampling works as it does upright.

#### Keystone distortion

A flat symbol is tilted away at the bottom, so near modules look larger than far ones.

![Keystone input and its path through the pipeline](../images/standardqr/decode-input-keystone.svg)

1. Finder centres and module sizes: along a finder line that runs into the distance (here the left one), the module size differs at its two ends.
2. Finders' frame and dimension candidates: the frame is the one plane that fits the three centres and both lines' size changes.
3. Alignment search: the frame predicts where the alignment pattern sits and how the grid turns there. The parallelogram of the centres drifts away from it as the tilt grows.
4. Four-point transform: the three finder centres and the alignment centre anchor a four-point transform, which samples the grid.
5. Parallelogram or frame grid: if the anchored grid fails, the parallelogram grid is tried. With no alignment pattern found, the parallelogram comes first and the frame after it.

Perspective also makes a finder taller or shorter than it is wide, as here. The column cross-check accepts that stretch within a window relative to its row, and beyond it only if the rising diagonal also reads 1:1:3:1:1, which a steeper tilt needs. Whenever the frame foreshortens, each finder line's count uses the geometric mean of its end sizes. On a version this small the plain mean snaps to the same size, and on a large one it would come up short. Here every finder column stays within its row's window, the shape's corner is right, and only three candidates are found.

#### Grey edges and wrong modules

The edges are anti-aliased or resampled, and a few modules read the wrong way.

![Input with grey edges and wrong modules, and its path through the pipeline](../images/standardqr/decode-input-degraded.svg)

1. Coverage re-read: if the grid fails, it is read again by coverage, which interpolates each module centre and splits it halfway between the two levels.
2. Matrix decode: Reed-Solomon corrects the wrong modules, up to each block's capacity.

Grey edge pixels fall between the histogram's two levels and turn on the grey-level stages. Each finder centre moves to the centroid of its centre square's darkness, a fraction of a pixel, and the module sizes are measured again to sub-pixel edges. Here the grid reads without the refined centres and sizes. At a lower density, a finder whose runs just miss 1:1:3:1:1 is measured again from the grey levels before it is rejected. Heavy blur and heavy damage are out of scope.

#### Thin or thick rings

A thin print, ink spread or a blurred ring cut by one threshold moves every dark edge the same way, here inward.

![Input with thin rings and its path through the pipeline](../images/standardqr/decode-input-thin-rings.svg)

1. Finder triple: through a finder's centre every dark run is shorter than its modules and every light run longer, so the column, the row again and both diagonals miss 1:1:3:1:1. Each is read again by its same-polarity edge distances, which a uniform shift of the dark edges leaves at 2, 4, 4 and 2 modules, and the finder must then also read along its rising diagonal, as a closed ring does.

The row scan still accepts only 1:1:3:1:1 and finds each finder on an off-centre row that reads that ratio. A finder whose edges moved by a quarter of a module or more, or that no row reads as 1:1:3:1:1, is not found (see [Input envelope](#input-envelope)). The first grid then reads.

#### Uneven lighting

A soft-edged shadow covers part of the symbol. The global threshold falls between lit and shadowed paper, so shadowed paper reads as ink.

![Input under a soft shadow and its path through the pipeline](../images/standardqr/decode-input-lighting.svg)

1. Binarization pass: when no single threshold splits ink from paper, the global passes read nothing and the regional pass runs, comparing each pixel with the mean black point of the blocks around its own.
2. Binarization pass: the regional pass binarizes the positive image first and runs the same path on it. Here that reads, so the negative is never binarized.

The result has only two levels, so the grey-level stages stay off: the centres are not refined and no grid is read by coverage. The regional pass is skipped in three cases: after a global pass gives a verdict on the content, for an image too small for one neighbourhood of blocks, and for a polarity it would binarize exactly as the global threshold did. A hard-edged shadow is out of scope.

#### Low density

A crisp render near one pixel per module has modules one or two pixels wide.

![Low-density input and its path through the pipeline](../images/standardqr/decode-input-low-density.svg)

1. Finder triple: the runs come out in whole pixels, one or two per module, too coarse for a ratio check. A crisp finder is accepted when the row above or below repeats its runs pixel for pixel and all 49 of its modules read through the edges its row and column measured.
2. Low density: for an upright or right-angle symbol, the module boundaries are read off the two timing patterns, finder to finder, and off the finders' own lines. The grid is sampled between them, each module wherever its edges fell.
3. Low density: both timing lines must read as timing patterns of the same dimension, which names the version.

This path is tried first for every corner. When it reads, nothing after it runs.

#### Light on dark

The modules are light on a dark background, as on a dark-mode screen.

![Light-on-dark input and its path through the pipeline](../images/standardqr/decode-input-light-on-dark.svg)

1. Binarization pass: in the positive image the finders' rings do not read 1:1:3:1:1, so the global positive pass reads nothing.
2. Binarization pass: the inverted pass decodes the inverted image, mirroring the histogram instead of counting it again, and runs the same path.

From the finder triple on, the path is the clean one.

#### Large version

The symbol is version 14 or up, in perspective, with the bottom-right alignment pattern lost, so the rest of the alignment lattice anchors a mesh.

![Large-version input with the alignment lattice, and its path through the pipeline](../images/standardqr/decode-input-large-version.svg)

1. Mesh over the alignment lattice: nothing anchors the four-point transform's fourth corner, so the mesh is decoded first. Without it, the parallelogram and its coverage re-read fail, and the frame grid reads after them.

An intact symbol reads through the anchored four-point transform, as in the keystone figure: a flat symbol in perspective is one projective map, which four correct points fix, while the mesh only interpolates between measured nodes. When the alignment search anchors the transform, the mesh runs after the transform and its coverage re-read, for what they do not read: a symbol bent off the plane, or a fourth anchor found on another mark.

From version 14 the alignment patterns form a lattice of 4 × 4 positions or more. The interior nodes are searched around a prediction passed on node by node from the finders, and missing ones again through a homography anchored on the three finder centres and the farthest node found. The row and column at coordinate 6 lie on the timing patterns and are not searched. Once the mesh is kept, they are extrapolated from the interior nodes. The mesh is kept when enough searched nodes are found, and each cell is sampled between its four nodes.

Versions 7 to 13 have a 3 × 3 lattice, two interior nodes per line, too few to extrapolate an edge line through. So the plane that best fits the finder centres and the found interior nodes places the row and column at coordinate 6 and any interior node not found. The same rule decides whether the mesh is kept, and it runs at the same point in the order.

### Support tiers

"Tier" is this project's shorthand for image-input difficulty, not standard QR terminology. The tiers were the implementation stages. Tiers 1 and 2 have a measured envelope that tests hold. Tier 3 is measured against other readers and has none:

| Tier | Input class | Status |
|---|---|---|
| Tier 1 | Clean images: screenshots, rendered QR codes, flatbed scans, arbitrary rotation, mirroring, reflectance reversal, a shading gradient or a soft-edged shadow over part of the symbol (limits under Lighting below). No meaningful perspective distortion | Supported |
| Tier 2 | Tier-1-clean images in perspective (keystone): a 4-point homography anchored on the alignment pattern the finders' frame predicts, that frame itself where nothing anchors the fourth corner, plus the piecewise mesh for version 7+ | Supported within the measured envelope, see [Input envelope](#input-envelope) |
| Tier 3 | Camera photographs: strong perspective, hard-edged shadows, blur, glare, a curved or damaged symbol, a symbol on a screen | Read as the sets under [Photographs](#photographs) show, with no envelope promised (see [Why](#why)) |

Matrix-level decoding takes an exact module matrix as input, so the tiers apply only to the image level.

### Supported

| Area | Coverage |
|---|---|
| Versions | 1–40 |
| ECC levels | All |
| Segment modes | Numeric, Alphanumeric, Byte, Kanji (JIS X 0208, written by the generator for text JIS X 0208 holds) |
| ECI | ISO-8859-1, UTF-8, Shift_JIS (ASCII, JIS X 0201 half-width katakana and the JIS X 0208 cells Kanji mode reads) |
| Text handling | UTF-8 BOM, multi-segment streams, and a Byte segment with no ECI header read as UTF-8, Shift_JIS or ISO-8859-1 by its bytes ([Decisions](#decisions), Byte-mode charset heuristic) |
| Structured Append | The header is read wherever it sits in the stream and reported as `QRCodeDecodeInfo.StructuredAppend` (0-based index, count, parity). Each symbol yields its own part of the text, and the caller reassembles the parts (rules on `QRStructuredAppend`). A header past its count, a second header, or a truncated one is `InvalidBitstream`. A part is text, not bytes, so if a set's encoder cut the byte stream inside a multi-byte character, the decoded text shows it: where the symbols declare UTF-8, U+FFFD appears at both edges of the cut, and where they declare nothing, the Byte segment on each side is read by its own bytes (the charset is resolved per Byte segment, and one that is not valid UTF-8 is read as ISO-8859-1, or as Shift_JIS where the guess holds). Both are the byte-segment decoder's own behaviour, checked by `ByteSegmentAndEciBoundaryTest` (`DeclaredUtf8_WithInvalidBytes_SubstitutesRatherThanFallingBackToLatin1`, `InvalidUtf8_FallsBackToLatin1`, and `UnspecifiedCharset_IsResolvedPerByteSegment` for a valid and an invalid segment in one stream). This library and the pinned encoder oracles cut between characters. Returning a part's bytes would be new public surface, added on a request rather than ahead of one |
| Image transforms | Arbitrary rotation, mirroring, reflectance reversal (light-on-dark) |
| Lighting | A shading gradient, or a soft-edged shadow (its edge a few modules wide) over part of the symbol, on images at least 33 px a side (measured limits under Lighting below). It is read through a regional binarization, tried after both polarities fail on the global threshold (see [Lessons Learned](#image-detection-and-sampling)) |
| Perspective (Tier 2) | Keystone to 40 % at 3-6 px/module and to 20 % from 2 px/module in every version, see [Input envelope](#input-envelope) |

### Unsupported

These are detected and reported, never misdecoded:

- FNC1
- Other ECI charsets

### Input envelope

The envelope covers the Tier 1 and 2 inputs above, with perspective limited to the measured keystone envelope below. Photographs are measured apart, under [Photographs](#photographs). Reflectance reversal (light-on-dark) costs one inverted retry. Non-square modules from thermal printers and laser markers decode within the envelope shared with the other symbologies ([qrcode-symbologies.md](qrcode-symbologies.md)).

A crisp render (every pixel wholly dark or light, the symbol along the image axes) reads from 1 px/module, whole or fractional. Anti-aliased or resampled edges read from about 1.5 px/module, and rotated or keystoned symbols from about 2. One exception was seen and not rechecked: a crisp, evenly lit version 1 at exactly 1.95 px/module failed at levels L, M and Q (2026-09-23), while 1.93, 1.94, 1.96 and 1.97 read.

This table compares this library with other readers on the same images from the [image decode sweep](qrcode-test-fixtures.md#image-decode-sweep) (2026-09-28). The sweep has 400 cases, ten per version at a random level, with numeric, alphanumeric or URL-like payloads longer than the version below holds. Six libraries encode each case (four have an image writer, the last row), and each is drawn once per kind. zxing-cpp 0.5.2 and ZXing.Net 0.16.11 read the same grayscale buffer.

| Kind, px/module | This library | zxing-cpp | ZXing.Net |
|---|---|---|---|
| Crisp nearest-neighbour, random offset, 1.0-1.25 | 2,400 of 2,400 | 561 | 111 |
| Crisp, 1.25-1.5 | 2,400 | 2,076 | 759 |
| Crisp, 1.5-2 / 2-3 / 3-6 | 2,400 each | 2,370 / 2,387 / 2,400 | 1,896 / 2,185 / 2,346 |
| Anti-aliased path, 1.0-1.25 | 356 | 41 | 6 |
| Anti-aliased path, 1.25-1.5 | 2,371 | 1,655 | 445 |
| Anti-aliased path, 1.5-2 / 2-3 / 3-6 | 2,400 each | 2,328 / 2,399 / 2,400 | 983 / 1,669 / 2,226 |
| Bilinear upscale of a 1 px/module image, 1.5-2 | 2,400 | 2,213 | 549 |
| Bilinear upscale, 2-2.5 / 2.5-3.5 | 2,400 each | 2,393 / 2,385 | 1,319 / 1,648 |
| Downscale of an 8 px/module image, 1.5-2.5 / 2.5-4 | 2,400 each | 2,394 / 2,399 | 1,440 / 1,998 |
| Right-angle turn / mirrored, crisp, 1.5-3 | 2,400 each | 2,400 / 2,394 | 2,053 / 2,058 |
| Supersampled at any rotation, 2-3 / 3-6 | 2,400 each | 2,354 / 2,400 | 1,143 / 1,922 |
| Supersampled, keystone up to 6 % (2-6) / 6-20 % (3-6) | 2,400 each | 2,400 each | 1,466 / 865 |
| JPEG quality 50-90, crisp, 2-4 | 2,400 | 2,394 | 2,160 |
| Each encoder's own image writer | 1,600 of 1,600 | 1,595 | 1,298 |

zxing-cpp reads 18 renders this library does not, all anti-aliased at 1.0-1.25 px/module, below the envelope. This library reads 3,607 that zxing-cpp does not. On the first baseline (2026-09-21, seven encoders) zxing-cpp read 2,002 of 63,600 renders this library did not, nearly all in five kinds: anti-aliased edges at 1.25-1.5 and at 1.5-2 px/module, bilinear upscales at 1.5-2, any rotation at 2-3 and keystone 6-20 %. The lessons below record what closed each. On the real images the gap is 28 reads of 548, each with a recorded cause ([qrcode-test-fixtures.md](qrcode-test-fixtures.md#where-the-gap-stands)).

When rings print or read thicker or thinner than their modules (ink spread, a thin print, blur), a finder is found as long as every dark edge moved by under a quarter of a module and some row through it still reads 1:1:3:1:1. Symbols whose dark edges all moved by 0.1, 0.15, 0.2 and 0.24 of a module read 590, 560, 408 and 144 of 600 (versions 1-10, 3-6 px/module, turned 0-60°, grey or binarized).

The next table is the measured keystone envelope (Tier 2). The keystone shortens one edge of the symbol by its share of the width, and the symbol is drawn with 2 × 2 supersampling at any turn. Each cell holds ten payloads of each version from 1 to 40 and counts the renders read, with zxing-cpp 0.5.2 (`TryHarder`) on the same images in brackets:

| Keystone | 3-6 px/module | 2-3 px/module |
|---|---|---|
| Up to 6 % | 400 of 400 (400) | 400 (388) |
| 6-20 % | 400 (399) | 400 (376) |
| 20-30 % | 400 (397) | 390 (327) |
| 30-40 % | 400 (242) | |
| 40-50 % | 397 (29) | |

The three renders still failing at 40-50 % are at 48-49 % keystone. Each selects a triple holding a false candidate, and the drawn triple, next in line, is not verified. Two were first blamed on a count further from the dimension than the timing match searches, but a 2026-09-28 re-measurement over 40,000 envelope renders found no drawn triple's count that far off. The 47 drawn triples left unverified (each the first or second alternative, its estimate within 4.5 modules) fail because their timing patterns do not read through their own frame. At 20-30 % and 2-3 px/module, eight of the ten failures miss a finder at about 2 px/module whose falling diagonal does not read 1:1:3:1:1, a low-density limit of the finder that reading rings by their like edges did not move.

On the same one-axis renders (2026-09-25), ZXing.Net and CodeGlyphX (given 1 s an image) read:

- 3-6 px/module: 296 and 106 up to 6 %, 142 and 7 at 6-20 %, 35 and 0 at 20-30 %, 8 and 0 at 30-40 %, and none at 40-50 %.
- 2-3 px/module: 155 and 25, 69 and 1, 9 and 0.

Mean times per image (one thread, wrappers included) for this library / zxing-cpp (`TryHarder`) / ZXing.Net were 0.30 / 2.06 / 5.3 ms up to 6 %, 0.34 / 2.23 / 7.6 at 6-20 % and 0.97 / 1.90 / 9.4 at 30-40 %.

The next table tilts the plane about both axes, turning the narrowing from the symbol's own vertical to any direction or toward a corner (45° off an axis). It was measured on another payload set, where renders narrowed at the top edge read 400, 400, 399 and 398 at 3-6 px/module and 393 at 2-3, and renders narrowed at any of the four edges read 400, 400, 399, 395 and 391. The renderer tilts the plane about any axis with the same depth ratio, 1/(1 − k), and with no tilt draws the old path's image bit for bit. Every module centre, mapped through the transform the renderer reports, lands on the module's colour. Where zxing-cpp reads a render, its corners lie a median 0.15 to 0.3 module from the drawn ones.

| Keystone | Tilted in any direction | Toward a corner |
|---|---|---|
| 6-20 %, 3-6 px/module | 400 (398) | 400 (400) |
| 20-30 % | 399 (400) | 400 (396) |
| 30-40 % | 399 (302) | 400 (237) |
| 40-50 % | 398 (137) | 398 (107) |
| 20-30 %, 2-3 px/module | 393 (366) | 394 (363) |

At 3-6 px/module the full sweep's candidate list holds every drawn finder of 9,600 but one (at 6-20 %, in a render that reads), so the triple fails, as along an axis. In four renders the drawn triple is an alternative past the two that are verified, in one it is the first alternative and does not read, and in one the stride pass left a finder out of the list. At 2-3 px/module seven drawn finders of 2,400 are not candidates because, as along an axis, the falling diagonal or the row again refuses them at about 2 px/module. Five renders select the drawn triple, count it right and fail after it, and one has the drawn triple fifth.

Lighting was measured on symbols printed with ink at 30 and paper at 220 (about 7:1), cropped to the symbol and its quiet zone, with a shadow edge three modules wide and light from eight directions. The symbols are Standard QR versions 1-5 at every level, and Micro QR M2-M4 and rMQR R7x43, R11x27 and R13x43 at both levels, at varied sub-pixel placements. Only renders that read under even light are counted (a turned symbol near its density limit can fail at some placements unlit, which is geometry, not light).

Every sweep held to the bounds below. A single placement often reads further, so they are measurements, not a contract. For the same reason the README and the public remarks carry no number: each number put there kept needing a condition it did not state (density, anti-aliasing, rotation, contrast, margin). They say "a shading gradient or a soft-edged shadow over part of the symbol", and the limits are here:

- Under a linear ramp that takes 80 % of the light across the image, a crisp symbol at 4 px/module reads in every direction, except rMQR R7x43, which loses 2 of 8.
- A crisp symbol along the image axes reads under a 40 % shadow from 2.6 px/module, and from 2 in all but a few renders in a thousand (a render that is exactly the grid and its quiet zone reads to 42 % and first fails at 43-44 %, on small Standard QR versions).
- A crisp turned symbol reads under a 40 % shadow from 3.6 px/module, except Standard QR version 1 turned near 45° with the light along the diagonal, which loses up to about 1 render in 200 from 38 % (none at 36 %).
- Anti-aliased edges, turned or not, read the same from 4.5 px/module, and from 3.5 in all but a few renders in a thousand. Micro QR M4 turned near 220-225° with the light toward 45° also loses a few in a thousand at 40 % (none at 36 %). Below that density losses start early: from 30 % at 3 px/module turned, and at 2 px/module from about 4 % at some sub-pixel placements.
- Lower contrast holds less: ink at 60 on paper at 200 holds to about 30 % and ink at 100 on paper at 170 to about 17 %, and from there to 37 % and 23 % a few turned renders in a thousand are lost.
- A margin wider than the quiet zone makes the global threshold split lit paper from shadowed paper instead of ink from paper. The regional pass reads most of what that loses, but turned version 1 symbols lose renders from 36 % with 2 extra modules, other symbols from about 27 % with 12 or more, and from 26 % at 8 px/module, where the modules line up with the blocks (below).
- Micro QR M1 holds the same 40 % shadow. Of 10,000 renders that read evenly lit, it reads 9,987 crisp along the axes from 2.6 px/module, 9,996 crisp turned from 3.6 and 9,998 anti-aliased from 3.5. The global threshold alone read 3,265, 101 and 0 (the regional pass refused M1 until its grids had to justify their corrections, see [microqr-decoder.md](microqr-decoder.md#lessons-learned)).

Deeper shadows read at some scales and not others. At 4 and 6 px/module, whole pixels along the axes, they read everywhere to about 54 %. Where the modules line up with the 8 × 8 blocks (8 and 16 px/module, whole pixels), every block is flat and takes its black point from the lit blocks above and to its left. Once the global threshold stops reading (between 45 and 48 % for the version 3 symbol tested, earlier for small versions), the regional pass reads only the directions whose shadow falls away from those blocks (4 to 7 of 8 from 48 to 60 %), as ZXing's own hybrid binarizer does.

At 4 px/module and 75 %, every reader measured here reads the version 3 symbol in only some directions (zxing-cpp and ZXing.Net included: 2 of 8). At 85 % none reads it, because its modules on either side of the shadow's edge share one neighbourhood. Larger versions and rMQR still read in some directions there. Reading past half on block-aligned modules is open. zxing-cpp reads none at 8 px/module.

On the same renders (2026-09-23, not measured since), this library read at least as many as zxing-cpp at 4 px/module at every depth and symbology probed (Micro QR shadow at 65 %: 5 of 8 directions against 1, and rMQR at 80 %: 5 against 0). At 3 px/module zxing-cpp read a few more Micro QR and rMQR renders (Micro QR shadow at 50 %: 8 against 6, and rMQR ramp at 80 %: 7 against 5), a class the sweep's kinds do not draw. An image under 33 px a side has no 5 × 5 neighbourhood of blocks and is read with the global threshold only.

#### Photographs

Camera photographs have no envelope. They are measured against zxing-cpp, image for image, on two sets and on photograph-like renders. The tables are in [qrcode-test-fixtures.md](qrcode-test-fixtures.md#where-the-gap-stands) (2026-10-10):

- ZXing's 179 QR photographs: 162 read against zxing-cpp's 165. Four that zxing-cpp reads are image failures here, and one read is this library's alone. Eleven of the 162 carry Shift_JIS in Byte mode with no ECI header.
- BoofCV's 536 photographs: 322 against 390. This library is within two photographs of zxing-cpp where the symbol is close, turned, in perspective, blurred, damaged or in shadow, and ahead under bright spots. It is furthest behind on a symbol on a monitor (7 against 17), uneven brightness (17 against 27), glare (12 against 21), a curved surface (25 against 34) and a high version (25 against 32).
- Renders through a pinhole camera: tilt to 55°, blur of 0.25 to 0.45 module, noise to 30 grey levels and a small symbol in a scene read as zxing-cpp reads them or better, and a bow of 1 to 4 modules reads 389 of 400 against 396. Barrel distortion is where this library falls behind, from about version 10.

No read on either set returned a text other than the expected one, or one another reader contradicted. Before the Shift_JIS guess of 2.0.0, the eleven Shift_JIS photographs came back as their ISO-8859-1 reading. Most of the gap is the search at full size: 41 of BoofCV's 77 gap photographs read once the image is scaled down, and 69 read as a grid through zxing-cpp's corners.

The README and the API docs name no other reader for the photographs this decoder does not read. That choice is the caller's.

---

## Why

- Tiers 1 and 2 are promised and photographs are measured. An input class joins the envelope when a set shows it reads and a test can draw it, which is how the decoder was built: stage by stage, against images another reader reads. Until 2026-10-10 this record called photographs out of scope without having measured them. The library stays dependency-free and auditable, so it uses no learned detector.
- The decoder is built on the encoder's own tables, so the two sides cannot drift apart. It reads the encoder's per-version placement tables (`ModulePlacer.GetLayout`, built by the reference function-pattern painters) for its blocked-module map, and the format-information decoder matches against patterns from the encoder's `GetFormatBits`. Codeword extraction also reads the encoder's placement runs. The cost is that a round trip can no longer catch a wrong table, because both sides would be wrong together and only another reader would fail. So the per-module zigzag walk stays in the assembly as the reference: it reads neither `Ops` nor `Index`, and `QRMatrixDecoderExtractParityTest` checks the run walk against it for every version and mask.
- Round-trip testing strengthens the encoder. Every `Create` output can be verified in-process (`encode → decode == input`) without ZXing. With the ZXing-decodes-our-output and ours-decodes-ZXing-output tests, both directions are cross-validated against an independent implementation.
- Decoding fails closed, because a wrong decode is strictly worse than a failed one. Reed-Solomon correction re-verifies syndromes after applying corrections, and format decoding requires Hamming distance ≤ 3 (the BCH(15,5) correction bound).
- Decoding allocates nothing in steady state. Matrix decoding uses stackalloc below 512 working bytes and `ArrayPool` above. Codeword extraction shares the encoder's per-version placement tables (built once per version used) and adds only one 1,152-byte mask table for all 40 versions, none per version or mask. The `Span<char>` overloads complete with no heap allocation (verified by a Release-only test).

---

## Decisions

| Decision | Choice | Revisit when |
|---|---|---|
| Version | On the matrix path the size gives the version exactly. On the image path the dimension estimate snaps to the nearest valid size, and the version information blocks (version 7 and up) are also read. They were first judged to matter only on heavily damaged symbols, wrongly: clean anti-aliased renders at 3 to 4 px/module put the estimate two or more versions off, and the blocks let them read (see [Image detection and sampling](#image-detection-and-sampling)) | - |
| Codeword extraction | Walk the encoder's placement runs, chosen for memory rather than speed. On x64 the per-module walk took 104 to 150 µs at versions 39 and 40, and three table forms were measured against it. The fastest, the encoder's stream-order index with a cached mask stream per version and mask, took 9.0 to 9.5 µs, but its mask streams stay resident and grow with every version and mask seen (29.6 KB at version 40, 441 KB at worst), and each decode streams 59 KB of index. The run walk took 10.2 to 11.1 µs, reads 6.5 KB of ops per decode and adds 1,152 bytes in total, because the mask bits under one output byte depend only on the pattern, the walk direction and the row and column phase. Reading `QRCodeData`'s packed bits directly to skip the unpack took 14.9 to 15.1 µs against 11.3 for the byte walk behind a vector unpack, and would be a second kernel to keep in parity, so it was not taken. ARM64 refuted it too (Apple M2, 2026-09-21: 1.18x to 1.28x slower end to end at version 40, 1.07x to 1.10x at version 1, faster nowhere, with the x64 kernel figures reproduced within a few percent). The browser is unmeasured, and no ordering is claimed there | - |
| Matrix decode performance | Stopped once further gains would no longer show when reading an image. After the extraction, reader and ARM syndrome changes, a version 40 Byte symbol decodes in 15 µs on x64 (extraction about 10.5, deinterleave 1.8, Reed-Solomon 1.3, the rest under 1.5) and 16.7 µs on an Apple M2 (10.2, 2.5, 2.5), down from 170 µs when the round started. Extraction is 60 to 70 % of it. Three candidates remained: a bit-plane extraction kernel as in rMQR (estimated 6 to 8 µs with PEXT on x64. A 177-row column needs 8-row bands, and ARM64, having no PEXT, would have to gather rows that sit a row apart in memory), five Numeric groups per window load (about 2 µs on one payload kind), and the deinterleave loop (never opened). Reading a version 40 symbol from a clean synthetic image takes 380 to 480 µs on x64 and a version 6 one 11 to 23 µs, and the matrix decode is 3 to 4 % of either, so each candidate is worth 1.5 % of a read or less. They were closed on that measurement, not on their own merits. They matter only to callers that decode a `QRCodeData` or a module matrix directly (the verify-what-I-just-encoded path, already 11x faster). For any other caller the next microsecond is in the image path | Such a caller turns up with a profile |
| Image path performance | Stage by stage, under one rule (the same result, bit for bit), until the profile ran out of stages. Between 2026-09-21 and 23 the threshold fill, the inverted retry, the piecewise mesh sampler and the finder search (its cross-check walks, their bounds and the row kernel) were each rewritten, each time keeping the replaced stage as the reference: the same threshold and grey levels, the same candidates, the same sampled pixels, and so the same text, status and corners on every fixture. Nothing resident grows with the images seen (the finder's edge buffer and the ARM64 histogram lanes are one rental per call), and the not-found path got faster on both machines. Each verdict was taken per input class, because hard-edged, fractional-pitch, soft and rotated renders stress different branches of the same stage. A version 40 symbol from a clean render at 3 px/module went from about 527 to 94 µs on x64 (`QRCodeImageDecodeEndToEnd`, span entry, BenchmarkDotNet means) and from 782 to 115 on an Apple M2 (stage harness). A 740 × 740 image with no symbol went from about 2,700 to 1,400 and from 3,827 to 1,756, and a smooth gradient from 1,776 to 322 and from 2,274 to 321. Version 6 moved less (20.6 to 10, and 34 to 11.6), because the stages that got a vector form never dominated a small image | What is left, each sized so the next round starts from a number. On an image with no symbol, three quarters of the row kernel's time is the coverage measurement on near misses (5,228 per polarity on 740 × 740 noise on the M2). Every kernel pays it, and no round has looked at it. The `SKBitmap` conversion is 6 to 13 % of a bitmap decode at 3 and 4 px/module and 13 to 28 % at 8 px, although its kernel was already made 14x to 30x faster. An image whose two values are not 0 and 255 (a symbol drawn #222 on #EEE) never takes the histogram's counted path and costs what it did before. Version 20 rotated at 3 and 4 px/module decodes on its second attempt, about 45 µs of a 140 to 200 µs decode, which is a question for the retry order rather than any stage's speed. The matrix decode is 2 to 4 %, closed in the row above. The browser is unmeasured. No test in this repository catches three planted faults in the row kernel that only over-report windows, because the cross-checks refuse what those faults send |
| Format decoding | Only 32 patterns are valid, so they are matched exhaustively by Hamming distance instead of BCH syndrome decoding, which is simpler, branch-free and gives the minimum-distance decision directly | - |
| Failure diagnostics | When an image does not read, each level of the search reports its main path's attempt (the selected triple, the corner its shape names, the grids from the finders, the estimated dimension, the grid through the transform, the grid as sampled), unless another attempt reads or gives a verdict on the content. It does not report the failure that got furthest, which Micro QR and rMQR report. The format word names no version, so a grid sampled at a guessed dimension gets past it by chance and then fails at Reed-Solomon with its own dimension's version. Tried on 2026-09-30, the furthest rule reported symbols whose format information was destroyed as `DataUncorrectable`, one version too small ([qrcode-symbologies.md](qrcode-symbologies.md#internal-organization), the result rule) | A signal of its own that a grid lies on the symbol, such as a format word read with no bit corrected (by chance about 1 word in 1,000), measured the same way |
| Byte-mode charset heuristic | A Byte segment with no ECI header is read as UTF-8 if it validates (strict RFC 3629), since UTF-8 payloads are common. Otherwise it is Shift_JIS if the bytes are well formed Shift_JIS, hold no control character but tab, CR and LF, and hold either three half-width katakana in a row or a byte from 0x80 to 0x9F, which ISO-8859-1 text never holds. Otherwise it is ISO-8859-1, the standard's default. ASCII decodes the same in all three, so the rule can change only high-byte payloads. The Shift_JIS step came in 2.0.0: Japanese encoders write Shift_JIS in Byte mode with no ECI header (eleven of ZXing's 179 photographs), and those used to come back as their ISO-8859-1 reading. It is zxing-cpp's rule without three clauses that turn ISO-8859-1 text into Japanese (three double-byte characters in a row, exactly two half-width katakana, a tenth of the bytes being Latin-1 symbols), and with tab counted as text. A lowercase accented letter before another letter is a well formed pair, and French puts three in a row (`générée`, `Télémétrie`). Measured on the .NET SDK's messages, written by ZXing.Net with no ECI header (2026-10-10): none of 24,555 ISO-8859-1 messages in French, German, Spanish, Italian and Portuguese reads as Shift_JIS, where the three-in-a-row clause read 13 French ones so and zxing-cpp returns another text for 19. All 7,375 Japanese messages, their 7,995 lines and their 11,705 runs between ASCII characters read as written. A guessed pair with no JIS X 0208 cell fails the read with `UnmappedCharacter`, as in Kanji mode, rather than return a text nobody wrote | The rule has three known costs. ISO-8859-1 text with three characters from 0xA1 to 0xDF in a row (`ÄÖÜ`, `¼½¾`) reads as half-width katakana. Windows-1252 text is not ISO-8859-1, and its typographic apostrophe before a letter is a Shift_JIS pair: of 1,866 such messages 345 (338 of them French) stop reading one character a byte and read as Japanese, 21 of them refused, as zxing-cpp reads them. Kanji whose bytes are all ISO-8859-1 letters keep the ISO-8859-1 reading when no kana or commoner kanji stands in the segment (`薔薇`). A segment that declares its charset is never guessed. Revisit on a request to read Windows-1252 or the CP932 vendor rows |
| Structured Append | `Index` is 0-based, as on the wire, so `Index < Count` holds directly. A 1-based index invites an off-by-one `<=`. The header is accepted anywhere in the stream, because refusing one after its ECI would refuse symbols other readers accept and gain nothing. The encoder writes it first. `Index >= Count` is `InvalidBitstream`, the same class as a character count that overruns the stream. A set of one is accepted, though the encoder never writes one. The caller reassembles by four rules. Every symbol reports the same `Count` and `Parity`. Each index `0 .. Count-1` appears once. Texts are joined in index order. `Parity` identifies the set and is not a checksum to recompute, since a reader cannot know which charset the encoder XORed. No combine helper ships, because the policy it would fix (a missing symbol, a duplicate, a parity mismatch) could not be removed later | A request for a combine helper |
| Kanji mode | Decoded, because Japanese-market encoders emit it and a decoder that rejects those symbols leaves callers no way to read them. Since 2.0.0 the generator also writes it for text JIS X 0208 holds ([When Kanji mode is written](qrcode-symbologies.md#when-kanji-mode-is-written)), which changed nothing on this side. The Shift_JIS conversion uses a generated 16 KB JIS X 0208 table rather than `System.Text.Encoding.CodePages`, so no dependency is added. The mapping is JIS X 0208, not CP932 (they differ on seven cells). See [QR Symbology Architecture](qrcode-symbologies.md) | - |

---

## Lessons Learned

### Image detection and sampling

- Module size from a horizontal scan breaks under rotation. The finder detector's row runs grow by √2 at 45°, so the dimension estimate misses by a whole version step (the first implementation returned `NotDetected` for every 45° input). Module size must be measured along the finder-to-finder lines (dark-light-dark runs through the pattern centers), which rotation does not affect. The row-scan value is only a fallback for when those runs leave the image.
- The light-dark-light alignment signature matches every isolated dark data module. A dark module with light neighbors on all four sides is extremely common in data areas and passes both the horizontal triple and the vertical cross-check. One such false positive shears the sampling transform until ~50% of the modules are sampled wrong. Only the 5×5 dark border ring distinguishes the real pattern: all eight ring samples at ±2 modules must be dark.
- Ring validation must follow the grid axes. Along the image axes, the ±2-module ring corners land outside a rotated pattern and reject the true alignment pattern. That is how the fix that rescued keystone-only inputs broke rotation+keystone combinations, until the ring samples were taken along the grid axis vectors derived from the finders.
- Coordinate-6 lattice lines lie on the timing patterns, whose 1-module alternation floods the light-dark-light alignment signature with false candidates, so edge lattice nodes are never searched, only derived.
- Pixel-quantized module sizes bias the dimension estimate one whole version low. The dark-light-dark runs walk in 1-pixel steps and originally returned the first light pixel, which rounds the boundary up and overestimates the module size by a systematic +0.07..+0.25 px, so the finder distance divided by it undershoots the module count by several modules at small pixels-per-module. On a fixed 512 px canvas, version 14 (6.32 px/module) read as 13 and versions 17+ one lower, while 15/16 (near-integer px/module) happened to survive. That non-monotonic pattern looked style-dependent but reproduced with plain black-and-white renders. The fix reports run boundaries at step − 0.5, centering the quantization error, and keeps the second-nearest valid dimension as a one-shot retry when the primary fails. A regression test decodes versions 12–25 on a fixed 512 px canvas.
- The finder triple is chosen by shape, because module size cannot tell a false finder from a real one. Data around the alignment pattern can form a 1:1:3:1:1 cross that passes every cross-check (its ring, a light module and two dark data modules. The vertical run is 1:1:5:1:1, inside the 50 % tolerance), and from 5 px/module up the row scan confirms it on more than one row.

  The selection used to score only neighbours in module-size order, by `spread / count`. At a whole number of pixels per module every candidate measures the same size, so the score was zero whatever the count and the tie went to scan order, leaving the real bottom-left finder out of both windows scored. The same tie mixed finders from two symbols of the same density in one frame.

  Every triple is now scored by its distance from a right isosceles triangle (from the squared sides, so rotation and mirroring do not matter) plus the relative module-size spread, with the confirmation count breaking ties. Nothing accepted before is rejected. A tie is anything within 0.05 of the best score, found in a second pass so small differences cannot chain. The first tolerance, 1e-3, was sized on exact renders: under keystone a false candidate at the square's fourth corner (any three corners of a square form a right isosceles triangle) scored 0.016 better than the real triple while confirmed on under a third of the rows. A differential sweep of 20,000 renders (flat, rotated, keystoned, two symbols) lost nothing and gained 364.

  The cost is cubic in the candidate count, but three candidates, the ordinary success path, return before any scoring. A full list of 32 with no good triangle takes about 41 µs with the two passes, and no noise image measured produced such a list.

- A count taken under a row stride is an undercount, so a poor triple chosen without the once-seen candidates is not an answer. At about 1.9 px/module a finder's 3-module band is 5 rows tall and the stride of 3 can hit it once, while a false candidate in the data is hit twice. Dropping candidates seen on one row left exactly three, returned unscored, and the symbol failed as `DataUncorrectable` on a bottom-left "finder" 15 modules from the real one.

  The selection now reports when it dropped such candidates and its triple scores past 0.25 (skew plus module-size spread. Flat real triples score up to 0.11, a triple holding a false candidate 0.33 and up), and the scan then covers the skipped rows, as when no triple is found. Crossing the bound only triggers a sweep, because keystoned real triples score past it too (up to 0.88 at 20 % keystone). The rows that confirm its finders also confirm false candidates inside the symbol, one of which can close a better triangle over one side, so the sweep's triple replaces the stride's only when confirmed over at least as much height in rows divided by module size (a false candidate of twice the module size is confirmed on as many rows as a real finder). Scoring the once-seen candidates directly, measured first, lost keystoned renders.

  Builder renders (versions 1-40, four levels, every size from 1.5 to 3 px/module) rose from 103,037 to 103,040 of 103,040, and 4,000 supersampled renders with keystone up to 20 % read identically, at 1.8 % more decode time on that set and none on flat renders.

- A finder in perspective is not square, so the column's window is set by the widest finder the envelope draws. Past 30 % keystone nearly every failing render failed because the finder at the wide edge was never a candidate (118 of 124 at 30-40 % and 3-6 px/module). A plane at keystone k stretches that finder by 1/(1 − k), 1.56 at 36 %. Each of its lines reads 1:1:3:1:1 on its own scale (a row of 33 px against a column of 49), but the column was refused for being 40 % or more from the row, a bound ZXing.Net, CodeGlyphX and go-qr share.

  Stretched along its own axes, a finder's column is at most that factor from its row at any turn, 2 at 50 %. Stretched off its axes it can be further, up to 2.31 at a stretch of 2 for any affine image of the rings. That needs no two-axis tilt: the keystone's slanted sides turn a corner finder's stretch 8-9° off its axes, and one-axis renders at 40-50 % drew columns up to 1.08 times the stretch. Over every tilt direction and turn at 50 % (version 40 with a 4-module quiet zone), the renderer's plane draws at most 2.24 along an axis and 2.27 in any direction. Whole-pixel runs on that finder at 3-4 px/module measure 2.33, and it stays a candidate, its rising diagonal reading.

  The column's window is 5/12 to 12/5, that factor plus a fifth for whole pixels, 3 % above the worst measured. The finder is taken on whichever row of its centre band passes, so the window need not reach the ratio at the centre. Over 3,234 renders near that geometry (versions 32, 36 and 40 at 48 and 50 %, tilted 96-108°, 3-4 px/module), narrowing the window to 2 loses a drawn finder in 565 renders, to 2.1 in 2, and to 11/5 in none. The row again, the same line through a refined centre, keeps 40 %.

  The bounded walk is derived for each window, so a refused column still stops at the first run no accepted cross section has. `FinderRunBoundsTest` checks both sets of bounds against the verdict. zxing-cpp allows 5 between any two of its four lines and walks up to four times the row with no early stop. With this window alone switched off, 30-40 % falls from 400 to 282 of 400 and 40-50 % from 397 to 189. The corpus's three `qrcode-2` gains come from it.

- A wider cross-check window admits noise, and a fourth line through the finder removes it. The wider window alone raised the candidates a full sweep keeps on 540 two-level noise images from 444 to 609, and the images yielding a triple from 60 to 84, each one more failed decode on an image with no symbol (20 8-bit noise images: 128 to 159 candidates). A plane-stretched finder is still an affine image of concentric squares, so every line through its centre reads 1:1:3:1:1, the rising diagonal included, while a texture cross fitting the ratio on its row, column and one diagonal rarely fits a fourth line. So a column outside the row's own 40 % is accepted only when the rising diagonal also reads. One inside it is judged as before, so no flat render can change. Noise came back to 474 candidates and the same 60 images with a triple, image for image (8-bit: 130, 14 as before). Keystone gained (40-50 %: 396 → 397, two more binarized keystone renders, and a flat binarized one no longer lost), because fewer false candidates mean fewer wrong triples.

- The dimension divides each finder line by its own two ends' sizes. A mean over both lines is wrong in two ways. Under the frame's model, the module count between two finder centres is exactly their distance over the geometric mean of the sizes at the two ends. The mean of the four sizes is larger by (w + 1/w)/2 on a foreshortened line: 13 % at a size ratio of 3, five versions at version 40, further than the timing match searched. An earlier round built this, saw it change nothing on sets where the stretched finder was never found, and removed it. Behind the wider window it gains 20 renders at 40-50 % (377 → 397 of 400).

  Its first form divided a line the frame takes as flat by the mean of all four sizes, and 15 of 4,000 binarized keystone renders that had read then failed: one line's whole-pixel runs were all one size, the other line's far end was 40 % larger, and that end, inside the flat line's mean, put a version 40 two versions short. Each line now divides by its own sizes whenever the frame is not the parallelogram, and by the mean of four only where it is, so every flat render stays as it was. The timing match searches around the same count. When shipped it lost one binarized render of 4,000, a version 28 at 2.3 px/module whose whole-pixel runs are ±9 % of the size, where neither estimate is the dimension (the mean says 134, the lines 138 and 134, the symbol is 129).

- Past 30 % keystone a triangle's shape cannot pick the triple, but the number of rows confirming each finder can. With every finder found, the selection failed: the stretched finder's row-scan size is up to twice the others', so the size spread that keeps false triples out penalized the real triple more than a false candidate inside the symbol, which also makes the better triangle with two real finders. The drawn triple ranked anywhere from second to 142nd.

  A finder's centre band is three modules tall whatever perspective does to its shape, and few rows repeat a false candidate. Ordered by the height (rows over module size) over which their least confirmed member was seen, the drawn triple came first after the selected one in every failing render. That order cannot replace the selection (three well-confirmed finders from two symbols are its best triple), so its first triple is decoded only after the selected one fails, and only once its two timing patterns read through its own frame. Through their frames the drawn triples read no timing module wrong. Triples holding a false candidate read 20 to 49 % wrong.

  Where the stride pass selected and returned, the list counts each finder on a third of its rows, once or twice, so the order is coarse. Three renders in 1,600 needed the second triple, so a failed decode verifies two. Verifying eight or 64 read none more. Sweeping the skipped rows before ordering made the first triple enough but doubled the benchmark's 740 × 740 noise (3.1 to 6.2 ms), as every failing attempt then paid for a sweep. The 512 × 512 noise it was first timed on, from another generator, did not show this. zxing-cpp keeps up to 256 triples in order of their longer leg and decodes each in turn.

  With this alone switched off, 30-40 % falls from 400 to 392, 40-50 % from 397 to 383 and 20-30 % at 2-3 px/module from 390 to 382. It also gave the four grey keystone renders of 4,000 gained below 20 %.

- A triangle's shape names the corner only while its hypotenuse is its longest side. The timing patterns always name it. Tilted about both axes toward the top-left finder, a plane draws that finder nearest and the finderless corner farthest, and past about 43 % keystone a leg of the image triangle outgrows its hypotenuse (1.10 times it at 50 % on version 40. Along an axis the leg never passes 0.82 of it). The vertex opposite the longest side, the rule every reader in `.references` uses, is then another finder, and every size, dimension and grid after it is built on the wrong corner. Toward a corner at 40-50 % keystone, 24 of 400 renders failed this way, each of which reads through its drawn grid. The count did not fail: from the wrong corner the estimate stayed within 3.2 modules of the dimension, and the timing patterns read in none of the 37 renders tilted toward a corner or in any direction. zxing-cpp weighs each side by the ratio of its two finders' sizes, its repair for a sample of this kind. With the near finder at the corner, both legs have the large end, and they grow.

  Three centres cannot identify the corner, since a projective map can put a triangle's right angle at any vertex. Only the true corner has both timing patterns running from it: from either other vertex one line crosses the data, and on flat symbols of versions 2, 25 and 40 neither reads. So when the shape's corner neither reads nor gives a verdict on the content, each other corner is decoded once its timing patterns read through its own frame, and an alternative triple picks its corner the same way, the shape's corner first. A read from the shape's corner costs nothing more.

  Toward a corner, 40-50 % went from 373 to 398 of 400, and in any direction from 385 to 398. The corpus's `qrcode-2/fix-finderpattern-order.webp` reads at all four turns, and no other envelope cell, sweep or corpus image moved. Switching off the selected triple's other corners alone loses all of the envelope's gain and the photograph. The alternatives' corner reads 19 more of 2,000 renders tilted toward the top-left finder at 40-50 % (10 at 2-3 px/module). Without the timing check first, every failed triple would pay two more decodes, 70-80 % on a failure.

  A content verdict from the shape's corner ends the triple, as a read does. Decoded from their two wrong corners, the drawn triples of 116,948 renders (versions 1-40, flat, keystoned to 30 % and tilted 44-50 % toward the top-left finder) gave 233,896 failures and nothing past Reed-Solomon. So a verdict there needs the same event that would give a read, and guarding the verdict alone would add a path nothing reaches.

- Whole-pixel runs cannot hold the 1:1:3:1:1 ratio on grey edges at about 2 px/module, and loosening the ratio is the wrong repair. An anti-aliased or resampled edge leaves a grey pixel, and whichever side of the threshold it falls on, the run is a pixel off its module. A 2.1 px light module covering 0.55 + 1 + 0.55 of three pixels reads 1 px under a threshold of 144 (Otsu puts it there because the edge greys fall into the dark class and raise its mean), outside the half-module tolerance, so the symbol is `NotDetected`. This hit all three symbologies and the builders' own anti-aliased rounded and circular finder shapes.

  Two other repairs were measured. A tolerance floor of 1.5 px reads those renders, but on 1-2 px noise it filled the candidate list (5 candidates to the cap of 32) and made the single-finder symbologies' failure paths 2-4x slower. Retrying the failed image at twice the size read slightly more and cost every unreadable image 2.5-18x.

  The shipped repair keeps the ratio and changes the measurement. Runs that fail by less than 1.5 px (the same budget on each of the five) are measured again from grey levels, in the row scan and all three cross-checks: each edge moves off its pixel boundary by the coverage of the pixels beside it, and the runs are held to the same half-module tolerance. The dark and light levels are the means of each threshold class's outer half, since the inner halves are the edge pixels being measured. An image with no pixel between the two levels would measure as its whole pixels did, so the second look is off for it, and two-level noise and crisp renders scan as before, candidate for candidate. From about 2.9 px/module the outer runs' half-module tolerance is the wider, so a finder there is never re-measured. On the three-module centre run the strict tolerance is wider at every supported density, so a window failing the strict check on its centre is never re-measured.

  The remaining cost is on grey texture with no symbol (blurred 1 px noise at 512 px: 1.1 to 2.1 ms `NotDetected`). It comes from the near-miss test on every window, not the measurement, and two restructurings did not move it.

  The near-miss tolerance is an absolute number of pixels, so the centre run gets the same budget as the outer ones, not three times it. Scaling it by run width, as the strict check scales its per-module tolerance, made a 1:1:1:1:1 run a near miss, and the review round measured it admitting a cross whose two axes read 1:1:3:1:1 and whose diagonal does not. The cross was still admitted afterwards, mostly not by the second look but by the diagonal's own ratio (next item).

- A finder's centre is the same share of every line through it, and the falling diagonal is held to that. A cross whose row and column carry the finder's runs and whose falling diagonal has a one-module centre passed the ratio on that diagonal: equal runs miss the tolerance by a tenth of a module on the centre, and the 45° walk adds the corner pixels beside it to the run. Over 10,496 anti-aliased renders of that cross at 2 to 4 px/module, 256 sub-pixel offsets each, the whole-pixel scan made it a candidate in 4,050 and the grey levels in 4,468. From 2.25 px/module up the two agreed. Below it the grey levels added 418, mostly through the axis cross-checks, which read the cross's bars correctly, and through the diagonal's coverage only at 2.0 px/module. The review's reading, that the coverage measurement admitted it by crossing module corners, held only for that last slice.

  The rising diagonal now also has to read when the falling diagonal's centre is under four fifths of the mean share the row's and column's centres are of their lines, on rows of 2 px modules or more (`IsDiagonalCentreShort`). Every line through concentric squares, or through an affine image of them, crosses the rings in the same proportions, and a thin or thick print moves every line's centre alike. The cross went from 4,468 candidates to 44. No read moved over 624 real images and the image decode sweep (54,400, 18,400 and 29,440 renders). The rule fired on 51 of 14,400 renders of a lone finder printed up to a fifth of a module thin or thick, or turned, and the rising diagonal read every one. Two-level noise went from 459 candidates to 439, and from 62 images yielding a triple to 59. 8-bit noise did not change.

  These were measured and not taken:

  - The rising diagonal on every candidate: noise down to 76 candidates, but three real images lost.
  - A fixed share instead of the axes' (a falling diagonal centre under 2.5 of its 7 modules): the cross down to 13, but two renders of a finder printed a fifth of a module thin lost.
  - The axes' share without the 2 px floor: four anti-aliased renders at 1.0-1.25 px/module lost, outside the envelope.
  - Refusing a candidate whose two diagonals both have a centre under 2.5 of 7 modules: the cross with both diagonals dotted from 4,505 to 22, but five anti-aliased renders of a real finder lost.

  A cross with both diagonals dotted still passes in 3,470 of 10,496 renders, because its rising diagonal reads as its falling one does. Like the one-diagonal cross, it stays a candidate and does not become a read:
  - Drawn alone at 2 to 4 px/module, neither cross was read by any of the three decoders, and neither was a lone real finder (0 of 336 renders each).
  - Beside a symbol, past its quiet zone (to the right, below, off the corner) at 2.5 to 5 px/module, every symbol read correctly with either cross there, as with a real finder there or nothing (720 Standard QR, 360 Micro QR and 360 rMQR renders per shape).
  - Inside a symbol's data it was not measured on its own. Random data with three planted finders kept every triple right.

- Between 1 and 1.5 px/module a crisp symbol holds all its information, but nothing built on ratios or finder centres reads it. A crisp render at a fractional scale, the builders' own or any nearest-neighbour resize, draws each module 1 or 2 px wide, a whole pixel or more, but two things the decoders rely on stop working. A run is up to a whole module off, so the 1:1:3:1:1 check's half-module tolerance refuses most finders (`NotDetected` on 57-73 % of crisp renders), with no grey to measure instead. A sample has (pitch − 1) / 2 to spare, an eighth of a pixel at 1.25 px/module, while finder centres are good only to half a pixel, so every grid extrapolated from a centre fails in the data. Both repairs read edges instead of measuring sizes.

  The finder is accepted as a whole pattern: its runs must have the shape a small crisp finder leaves (four runs of 1 or 2 px around one of 3 to 5), repeated pixel for pixel on a neighbouring row, and then all 49 modules are read through the six edges the row and column measured. That is exact where three ratios are not, and over 18 two-level noise images it admits no candidate the ratio scan did not. The shape test checks the centre run first because on fine noise it runs on every window, and the row comparison keeps noise from reaching the cross-checks. A render that passes the ratio is still accepted the old way, on three lines through the centre, so a finder with one ring module wrong is refused only where the ratio fails it.

  The grid is not fitted (`ModuleBoundaryReader`, shared by the three symbologies). A timing pattern crosses every module boundary past the finder, and a finder's centre line crosses four of its own. The two boundaries inside a three-module run (a finder's centre square, an rMQR alignment or corner pattern on the timing row) show in the modules in line with it, because a crisp module has no edge inside it. Each module is read at the middle pixel of the cell its boundaries frame, however wide it came out. A least-squares fit fills only the boundaries nothing crossed, and a line that does not read as a timing pattern refuses the whole table. While a module is at most 2 px, run lengths classify a run: one module is 1-2 px, three are 3-6, seven are 7 or more. So the single-module bound is 1.2 times the finder's module size, not the 1.6 of the fitted timing lines (at 1.6 a three-pixel alignment run on an rMQR timing row counted as one module, and the width came out two short). A least-squares grid through the same boundaries, tried first, left about a tenth of the renders below 1.25 px/module unread. The table leaves none.

  The table applies below 1.75 px/module, measured at the finder, on symbols along the image axes (any right angle, mirrored or not). For Standard QR and rMQR it comes before the fitted grids there (Micro QR tries its fitted frames first, and their corners held in every builder render): where both read, the table's corners are the symbol's own edges while the fitted grids' are extrapolated to within a module, and for rMQR the perspective search could otherwise spend the whole attempt budget first. The table does not read anti-aliased input at this density, where a module centre covers well under half of any pixel. The coverage reading through the grey-level frame (below) reads some of it, 356 of 2,400 sweep renders at 1.0-1.25 px/module where 36 read before, and it stays outside the envelope.

- Measure between edges of the same polarity. The module size used to be the finder's outer-to-outer span through its center (7 modules), but grey edge pixels on one side of the threshold move a dark-to-light and a light-to-dark edge in opposite directions, so that span included both shifts. One pixel of ink spread at 3 px/module is +4.8 %, 4.8 modules over a version 24 span, and v20-v37 read one or two versions low (lighter edges read them high). The error is an asymmetry, not noise, so averaging more such spans does not remove it. The dark ring's inner edge on one side and outer edge on the other are 6 modules apart whatever the bloom. Pairing them twice per line took the mean error from +0.4..+1.4 % to within ±0.3 %. It does not narrow the spread from pixel quantization along a rotated ray (still about 5.6 % at 3 px/module), which is why the version information is also read.

- A ring printed or read too thick or too thin keeps the distances between its like edges, and the cross-checks read them. Ink spread, a thin print, a blurred ring cut by one threshold, and a screen's glow read inverted all move every dark edge of a finder the same way, so its dark runs are all longer or all shorter than their modules and the line's own 1:1:3:1:1 check refuses it, most often on a diagonal (3, 7, 13, 6, 3 px at 5 px/module). The distance from each edge to the next same-polarity edge stays 2, 4, 4 and 2 modules. A cross-check line the ratio refuses is read by those four distances, each held to half a module (the ratio's own margin), with the fitted shift under half a module a run and a module of at least 2 px.

  Candidates on 540 two-level noise images changed as the conditions were added:

  - Read this way on every line, the row scan included, with the shift allowed up to a whole module and no floor: from 442 to 1,220.
  - With the bound and the floor, the row scan keeping the ratio (so the same windows reach the cross-checks), and a line's shift held to the row's sign (one print or one blur moves a finder's edges one way): 518.
  - With a finder any of whose lines needed like edges also reading its rising diagonal (a real ring is closed): 459.

  The walk's side cap allows these lines the largest ratios their conditions permit: a side run under 16/19 of the centre and a third of the total, which on the column never passes the ratio's own cap. A correct but looser cap, 25/19 of the centre, made successful reads 4 to 5 % slower. The tight one costs about 3 % at most. The centre bound did not grow: these lines' centres are 0.28 to 0.57 of the total up to 90 px, inside the ratio's 0.21 to 0.64.

  Against the decoder before it, the results were:

  - Real images: 391 to 401 of 548, none lost.
  - The synthetic sweeps: identical, but for one render gained.
  - Symbols whose dark edges all moved by 0.1 to 0.24 of a module: 1,260 to 1,702 of 2,400, one lost.
  - Binarized renders, flat, keystoned to 20 % and tilted to 50 %: +110, +127 and +127 of 4,000 each, with 3 tilted ones lost.
  - At 40-50 % keystone: +1 and −2 of 800, one of them traced to a false candidate in the data that now completes a better triangle.

  These were not taken:

  - The runs corrected by the fitted shift and held to the ratio (16 more real-image reads, 1,270 noise candidates).
  - The distances held to half a module per module of distance (+10 net, 8,659 noise candidates).
  - A 2.5 px floor (loses `qrcode-3/30`).
  - Separate caps for light and dark side runs (16/19 and 4/13, 5/7 and 1/3, no faster than the one cap).
  - The like-edge module size for the candidate (no read moved).

  The rising diagonal costs one read, `qrcode-3/30` at 270°.

  A finder whose every row misses the ratio, as a uniform spread along the image axes draws it, is still not found. With the row scan also reading like edges, the shifted symbols read 1,841 of those 2,400 instead of 1,702, but noise gave 471 candidates, failures ran 11 % slower on the same row kernel, and a knife-edge photograph was lost, so it is a lead whose cost in the edge-list kernel is to be measured first. The ring's closure, which another reader checks once its run tests pass, was the lead for a finder lost near 2 px/module. The corpus had none, and it was not taken.

- A symbol's stated version beats an estimate of it. Versions 7+ carry their version twice, BCH(18,6)-protected, each copy within 7 modules of a finder, and since the grid is anchored on the finder centers, a matrix sampled at a dimension several modules off still reads them (4 modules off at version 27 moves them a quarter of a module). The image path reads them from the failed sampling and tries the dimension they name before the runner-up. Near the axis at 3 px/module the estimate was measured up to 9 modules off. The snap is clamped to versions 1-40, because an estimate just past 177 modules used to round to 41 and come back `NotDetected`.

  Reading the blocks through the first transform before sampling, to verify a triple, was analysed and closed without being built (2026-09-28). Through a grid anchored on the finder centres, a dimension Δ modules off moves a block about 7·Δ / (dim − 7) modules, a whole module at Δ = 16 near version 30, so that read misses where the count is far enough off to need it. The blocks are 5 to 7 modules from their nearest finder, whose own axes and sizes would place them. The case it was for, a drawn triple whose count lies outside the timing match's ±16 modules, occurred in none of 40,000 envelope renders and none of the corpus gap, and the 47 renders whose drawn triple is not verified also read their version blocks right through the first transform, so a dimension-independent read would add nothing. As a triple check it is weak: a copy within 3 errors of a codeword is about 13 % of random 18-bit words. Rejecting a triple whose version disagrees with its count was not taken either, because `TimingPatternsRead` already refuses false alternatives and a real symbol whose version blocks alone are damaged still decodes through the timing dimension.

- The alignment checks had been calibrated on the biased module size. Correcting it turned 11 rotated renders from reading to failing, all in the alignment search, whose result changed when the module size moved by under 1 %. Three defects stacked:

  - The search took the first hit in scan order, so a false pattern to the left won while the real one sat 0.1 px from the prediction on the same row.
  - It compared each run with the plain module size, although at 45° a row's run through a module is √2 times longer.
  - Each run on its own gained or lost the bloom pixel.

  The search now keeps the hit nearest the prediction and re-centers it on its own row (row hits near the pattern's edge cut its center short and lean toward the prediction), derives the expected run length per scan direction from the grid axes, and checks each light run plus the dark center as a pair (same polarity again). It requires the light ring at ±1 module as well as the dark ring at ±2, because data around a real pattern was measured passing everything else 1.8 modules from it. On three sweeps the strict light ring beat both requiring at least 6 of 8 and requiring none.

- An anchor's resolution must be weighed against how far the transform extrapolates from it. At about 2 px/module the alignment pattern's centre is the midpoint of a 1-2 px run, resolved to a third of a module (found at 44.00 against a true 43.64), while the finder centres, 7 modules across, were within 0.14 px.
