The four-point transform reads that third of a module as perspective and extends it across the bottom-right block, putting 17 to 22 modules wrong on flat level-L renders that the three finders' parallelogram sampled with none wrong. So an alignment-anchored global transform that fails to decode is retried through the finders alone, only on the failure path. A keystoned symbol still decodes through the alignment anchor first.

  A failure-path cost must still be measured on failures. As first shipped, the fallback made the finder-found failures it was measured on 15-40 % slower (damaged data at 2-4 px/module, v2 to v40), because it decoded again where it could not help: at the true size a flat symbol samples identically through both anchors, and at the runner-up the grid is the wrong size either way. Skipping those two cases brought it within 10 % of the decoder without the fallback. This was measured, not reasoned: the first explanation, modules drawn 1 px wide, could not be right, because a non-antialiased fill covers a pixel whose centre lies inside the module, so flooring a true module centre always lands inside it.

- The parallelogram after an anchored grid is also read by coverage, as the four-point and frame grids are. It had been read only one pixel against Otsu, with no measurement behind the difference. A photograph of round finders and small round modules, its alignment pattern drawn as dots, anchors a fifth of a module off. The parallelogram through its finders fails one pixel against Otsu and reads by coverage with no correction, at every right angle. Nothing else in the corpus moved, 13 anti-aliased sweep renders at 1.0-1.25 px/module now read that neither reader read before, and nothing was lost. The cost is one coverage reading on a failing grey-level image whose anchored grid failed (measured 2026-09-28).

- Below 2 px/module a grey-edged symbol fails in its frame, not its pixels, and the grey levels place the frame. Sampled through the geometry they were drawn with, using the decoder's own reader (one pixel against Otsu), anti-aliased renders at 1.25-1.5 px/module read 2,388 of 2,400, where the decoder read 1,367. Its finders were a median 0.22 modules and up to half a module off, because a centre from thresholded runs is good to half a pixel, and the grid extrapolates that error across the symbol.

  A grey edge pixel's level is the share of it the module covers, so the darkness-weighted centroid of a finder's centre square is exact where a run is not (`ConcentricCentroid`). The window runs along the symbol's axes, ± 2 modules, ending inside the light ring, so its edge pixels are light and weigh nothing wherever the edge falls. This cut the error to a median 0.044 modules, and the three finders' parallelogram read 2,261 of the 2,400. The same centroid refines the alignment patterns and mesh nodes (± 1 module), for another 17 anti-aliased reads at 1.25-1.5 px/module and 35 keystoned ones from the mesh nodes, measured before the refinement was limited to grey-level images.

  Three details each cost reads when wrong:

  - The window's scale is each finder's own module size along the finder-to-finder lines. A finder's row runs grow by up to √2 under a turn, and a window scaled by them reached the dark ring and lost 427 turned and keystoned renders. One size for all three lost keystoned renders whose far finder measures 45 % larger than the near one (12 against 5).
  - The centroid takes two passes, the second centring the window. Below 1.6 px/module the light ring is under two pixels, and an off-centre window takes in more of the dark ring on one side (one pass left 11 of 36 test placements more than a tenth of a module off).
  - The module size the dimension estimate divides by is measured again from the refined centres, since the runs are read outward from them (keystone 6-20 %: 2,180 → 2,210 of 2,400).

  The centroid runs only on a grey-level image: on a two-level image the centroid of whole pixels is no finer than the runs, and on a camera-binarized photograph (`qrcode-3/04`) it moved a blobby centre square by 0.85 px and lost the image at all four turns. Binarized images, the regional pass's included, keep their run centres. Refining them too gained 12 real-image reads and 12 keystoned renders but lost that photograph at every turn and another through the regional pass, while refining only grey images loses nothing.

  These were refuted:

  - The whole finder as the window (± 4 modules, the dark ring's edges averaged in), a median 0.073 modules off against 0.044, and 2,096 of 2,400 reads against 2,261.
  - Darkness scaled linearly from the image's extremes instead of the class levels, 0.043 against 0.044, so the levels are not what limits it.
  - The dark area as the module size (√(area / 9)), within 2 % on anti-aliased renders but 15 % either way on crisp ones, where a square in whole pixels is not 9 modules.

  The refined frame costs grey version 40 reads 5 to 6 % (rotated and soft renders).

- One pixel against Otsu is the wrong reader for a grey edge, and the right reader runs as a second reading, not a new first one. On a blurred image Otsu sits above the midpoint of the two levels, because edge greys fall into the dark class, so a light module between dark ones reads dark. The coverage reading (`LuminanceSampler`) compares the luminance interpolated at the module's centre with the midpoint of the two levels. Through the true frame it read 2,399 of 2,400 bilinear upscales at 1.5-2 px/module, against 2,338 for one pixel against Otsu, and through the refined frame 2,399 of the bilinear and 2,367 of the anti-aliased renders at 1.25-1.5 px/module, against 2,336 and 2,261.

  It re-reads a grid that failed on a grey-level image, and the result is decoded only when it changes a module. A crisp image has no grey levels and one pixel reads it exactly, and a symbol that reads pays nothing. The limit is the failure path's cost in grids: Micro QR sends about 19,000 grids a failing image through Reed-Solomon, half with a format word within 3 bits, and reading all of those again took 8-bit noise to 1.78x and another symbology's image to 2-5.6x. A real symbol's format modules sit next to its finder, where the frame is best, and texture reads an exact word about 1 time in 1,000, so Micro QR reads a grid again only when its format word read exactly, which keeps 8-bit noise at 1.05x, for 6 of the 284 reads it gained at 1.25-2.5 px/module.

- Once the frame is accurate enough to sample the timing modules, they give the dimension. Blur and a turn break both ways of finding it: the finder runs measure the module size up to about 6 % off (a bilinear version 40 at 1.95 px/module measured 1.83), putting the estimate a version or more out, and at version 40 past the range, while under a turn at 2-2.5 px/module the counted timing runs can stop reading. So through the refined finders the grid of each dimension within four versions of the estimate is sampled along both timing lines, and the dimension leaving under an eighth of their modules wrong is tried where the estimate is refused and the count fails, and after the version information when the estimate's grid fails. The eighth tolerates a few damaged timing modules (four of a version 40's 322 painted over still reads) but not a broken line (a quarter painted over is `NotDetected`, as before). Two versions either way was not enough for the version 36-40 bilinear renders at 1.87-1.94 px/module.

- A blurred finder can be invisible at the global threshold, and the midpoint of the two levels finds it. A 1 px/module image scaled up bilinearly to about 2.45 px/module leaves the finder's light ring as one bright pixel (149, 252, 155 on a Micro QR M1). Otsu at 163, pulled up by the edge greys, makes the ring 1 px wide (runs 3:2:8:1:4), so no candidate is found and the symbol is `NotDetected`. At the midpoint, 146, the runs are 3:2:7:3:2. Micro QR and rMQR scan once more at the midpoint, last, after the regional pass, for each polarity whose strided scan and sweep found no candidate on a grey-level image.

  Both conditions were measured. Gated on no grid reading its format information, the scan ran on every other symbology's image, whose finders are found and fail (rMQR on a Micro QR image up to 2.9x). Gated on no candidate, it costs those images nothing. Placed inside each attempt, it ran on every symbol whose finder a shadow hides from the global threshold, before the regional pass read it (an M1 under a 55 % shadow 11.2 → 14 µs). After the regional pass it costs those nothing either, and the blurred finders it is for were `NotDetected` on `main`, regional pass included. Standard QR has no such scan: its sweep reads 4,799 of the 4,800 bilinear renders at 2-3.5 px/module without it, and the one left fails as it did on `main`.

- Count the modules where the symbol marks them, and measure only where it does not. A renderer that snaps each module to whole pixels draws them 2 or 3 px wide at 2.13 px/module, and a finder that lands on 2 px modules measures 2.0, 6 % off the symbol's pitch: two versions at version 29, too far for the version information to be read. The timing patterns alternate one module at a time between the finders, so their dark runs number 2v + 3 whatever width each module was drawn, and the two lines (row 6 and column 6) must agree. A line whose runs are not all about a module long refuses rather than miscounts, which a single painted-over timing module triggers. The count is a fallback, taken only once the estimate's sampling fails: tried first, it cost every successful decode 8 % for rare renders.

  A fallback must also be reachable from every early exit before it. The estimate refuses a dimension more than four modules past version 40, snapped finders at versions 39-40 measure a few percent small, which put a 177-module symbol there, and the refusal returned before the count ran.

- Use one pixel convention everywhere: integers are pixel edges, and the pixel containing a point is its floor. The finder centres were always in that convention (a run's end index is exclusive), but every sampler, in all three symbologies and both kernels, picked its pixel with `(int)(x + 0.5f)`, which reads half a pixel right of and below each module centre. Two anchors had the opposite half-pixel error and partly cancelled it: the alignment pattern's vertical centre (`+ 0.5` where the run's midpoint needs `+ 1`) and rMQR's sub-finder refinement. At 2.5 px/module and up the offset stays inside the module, so it went unseen. At 1 px/module it reads the neighbouring module every time (Standard QR 0 of 2,560 clean renders, rMQR 4 of 256, Micro QR 41 of 109), and at 1.5-2.2 px/module, where the builder's fixed-size renders land, it reads module edges (288 of 676 fixed-size renders across the three symbologies decoded). After the fix every 1 px/module render reads, and 666 of the 676. The rest were the builder's whole-pixel module snapping, covered by the timing-pattern lesson above.

  The offset also had an effect it should not have had. It points the same way as the finders-only corner's error when the top edge of a keystoned symbol is shorter, so version 1 past its 2 % envelope, and version 2+ with a missing alignment pattern, read further in that one direction (on a 20,000-render sweep, flipping the keystone turned `main`'s 19,871 into 19,721). Corrected, the two directions read alike.

- A symbol under a lighting gradient has no global threshold, and the second binarization is an added attempt, not a new first one. On photographs with a shading gradient across the symbol, a light module on the dim side is darker than a dark module on the bright side, so one threshold reads a whole side as one class and the finders there as solid. Every image of one real-image corpus set failed that way, as `NotDetected`.

  A regional binarization reads them (`LocalBinarizer`, the hybrid scheme of ZXing: an 8 × 8 block's black point comes from its mean, or from its neighbours when the block is flat, and each pixel is compared with the mean of the 25 around its block). Replacing the global threshold with it lost 14 reads elsewhere in a probe: it has no grey levels to give the finder's second look, and a block-local threshold moves edges the global one had right. Three binarizations were probed as that fallback on the real images:

  - A local mean over a tenth of the image, 8 % under it.
  - One over an eighth, 5 % under it.
  - The hybrid scheme, which read the most (359 of 548 against 353 and 356) at about half the cost and needs no integral image.

  It matched an independent port of ZXing's `HybridBinarizer` on 20,000 random cases in three SIMD configurations.

  So it runs after both global polarities have failed, in both polarities (`RegionalRetry`), each binarized from its own pixels. The flat-block rule reads a block as paper, and the paper of a light-on-dark symbol is dark, so inverting the positive's regional output reads 2 of 48 such renders, where binarizing the negative reads 44.

  A polarity is decoded only when its regional binarization moves a pixel out of the class its own global threshold put it in. An image of only 0 and 255 is not binarized at all, because every regional threshold then lies in [0, 251], so neither polarity can differ. Both 0/255 noise and a black-and-white crisp symbol that failed on its data pay nothing more. The skip is exact, not tuned. The share of pixels a regional binarization moves does not separate reads from costs: reads range from 0.5 % on Micro QR photographs to 51 % on `qrcode-5`, and inside that range lie 8-bit noise at 0.6 %, another symbology's image at 0.02 to 2.3 % and a textured ramp at 40 %. A count of blocks with a quarter moved does not separate them either, and any bound would have lost reads or kept the cost.

  Any other image pays up to two binarizations, plus a decode for each polarity whose binarization moves a pixel. A binarization takes about 0.09 ms at 512 × 512, and the negative's is skipped once the positive's decode reads. Both are read from the positive, the negative complemented as it loads, and written into the one buffer the inverted retry rented. (Binarized into a second rented buffer, the negative allocated an image-sized array on every failing large image where the shared pool stops at 1 MB: .NET Framework, .NET Core 5 and earlier.) Noise of two levels more than 24 apart moves no pixel, since every block holds both levels and its threshold falls between them. Two levels closer than that make every block flat, which reads the lighter level as paper, and the darker one too unless it is 0. A large flat area of the darker level on the top or left edge, or of a level more than half the lighter one, can also move pixels.

  Against `main` before it, the results were:

  - The real images: 295 → 359 of 548 Standard QR reads (2 of them by the negative) and 60 → 64 of 64 Micro QR, none lost.
  - The synthetic sweep: +400 Standard QR reads (bilinear upscales at 1.5-2 px/module +154, anti-aliased edges at 1.25-2 +103, keystone past 6 % +74), +45 Micro QR (42 of them bilinear at 2-2.5), of which a refusal of regional M1 reads cost 36, leaving 9, until the evidence rule replaced it, and +11 rMQR.

  Gains on evenly lit images come from the same difference: a block-local threshold places grey edge pixels differently, so a symbol one threshold misses by a few edges can read at the other.

  Micro QR's regional pass at first refused, by level, what texture passed as: any M1 read, an empty read that needed correction, an M3-M or M4-M read at its limit. Each refusal cost real reads and left texture landing on the next level. The Micro QR evidence rule replaced them ([microqr-decoder.md](microqr-decoder.md#lessons-learned)): every grid, in every pass, uses only the corrections its structure justifies.

  The cost is up to two more decodes, one per polarity, on a failing image with grey in it: blurred noise, a gradient, another symbology's image, an anti-aliased symbol past correction. The multiple was largest where the global threshold fails cheaply. One threshold splits a ramp with ±20 noise and no symbol into two solid halves in 0.2 ms at 256 px, but under the regional pass the ramp became finder-like specks and cost Micro QR and rMQR 16 to 41 ms (80 to 200 times). ±8 noise leaves every block flat and costs nothing more. A textured ramp holding no symbol went 0.32 → 1.80 ms for Standard QR, and 21 → 88 ms and 25 → 113 ms for Micro QR and rMQR, whose every attempt is a strided finder scan followed, when that fails, by a full sweep.

  The regional attempts keep the sweep, because a strided scan misses a finder whose band falls between the rows it visits. A cut that skipped the sweep there lost 30 to 47 of each 880-render set of unevenly lit Micro QR and rMQR renders at 1.5-2 px/module to their position alone, although every measured set had shown no loss. The synthetic sets that turn a symbol or offset it by fractions of a pixel are evenly lit, so the global attempts, which keep the sweep, read those renders before the regional attempt runs. The unevenly lit set was axis-aligned, and no real image in the corpus had the case. Eight or more finder-like marks are a second case: they outrank the real finder in the strided list, which tries eight (1,254 of 12,288 renders with ten decoys read only with the sweep).

  The finder search's contract is that a decoder's envelope is never narrower than a full sweep's, and cost is not a reason to break it. The single-finder scan departs from it in one place, recorded as a residual: after a read too long for the destination it runs no sweep, so a call probing for its buffer size costs what a sized one does ([single-finder candidate scan](qrcode-symbologies.md#single-finder-candidate-scan)). The failure-path work addressed the cost instead, making failing Micro QR decodes on noise-like images 1.5 to 2.6 times faster and rMQR ones 4.8 to 7.3 times faster, with every result unchanged ([Micro QR](microqr-decoder.md#lessons-learned), [rMQR](rmqr-decoder.md#lessons-learned)).

- Under keystone the fourth anchor fails in its prediction, not its search, and the finders already show how far the symbol is from flat. Every keystoned render that failed at 6-20 % and 3-6 px/module read when sampled through the geometry it was drawn with, finder centres refined to within a tenth of a module. The parallelogram of the three centres put the bottom-right alignment pattern 17 to 30 modules off at versions 31-40, and the widening search anchored on the pattern one lattice step in. Version 1, with nothing to anchor, was sampled through that parallelogram and missed its far corner by up to 2 modules.

  Along each finder line a plane in perspective changes the module size: the size at one end over the size at the other is the square of the ratio of the two ends' projective weights. So the three centres and the four sizes at the ends of the two lines fix one plane (`FinderFrame`, exact to a hundredth of a module on any plane in `FinderFrameTest`). The frame is refused in favour of the parallelogram when the weights would put the vanishing line across the symbol. zxing-cpp reaches the same corner by intersecting lines fitted to the finders' ring edges, extrapolating seven modules of edge across the symbol. ZXing.Net corrects the parallelogram linearly and searches 4, 8 and 16 modules around it, CodeGlyphX searches one window at whole pixels and then by brute force, and go-qr samples affine only. None of them uses the change of size across the whole line between two finders, which the frame measures.

  Switching each part off alone when it shipped (2026-09-25) measured its worth: the prediction at the frame gave 130 of the sweep's 190 keystone reads gained and half the corpus's 34, the frame as the last grid 47 of the 190, and the timing match through the frame 47 of 400 at 40-50 %. Before the frame, the mesh seeded from the parallelogram had found 0 to 2 of its 16 to 36 nodes in all but two of the failing large renders. The mesh's first-row seeds from the frame changed nothing and were removed.

- A measurement's resolution decides where it may be used. The frame is only as good as the change of size it reads. Whole-pixel runs give sizes in twelfths of a pixel, a median 2 % off and up to 7 % on 400 keystoned renders, which put the frame's prediction up to 8 modules off at versions 31-40. Midpoint crossings of the luminance interpolated along the line give 0.5 % and up to 2 %, 2 modules at worst, well inside the lattice step. Darkness integrated along the line gave 1.3 % and up to 5 % (6.5 modules at worst), because it depends on the levels' calibration, while a crossing depends only on their midpoint. The centre refinement keeps its runs: sub-pixel sizes there too moved flat renders (anti-aliased at 1.0-1.25 px/module +49 −6), a lead for low density rather than keystone.

  So grey images measure crossings. A binarized image, whose edges are always whole pixels, uses the change its runs show only when it exceeds their resolution (more than four twelfths of a pixel between the two ends). Unbounded, two flat binarized renders at 2.6-2.8 px/module that had read before failed, among 4,000. A bound of two thirds of a pixel cost about 50 binarized keystone reads, and a bound of exactly a third let float rounding decide on the twelfths lattice (2 losses in 4,000 renders against none). Weighing a binarized image's runs at all is its whole keystone gain (323 of 4,000 when they shipped).

  The two ends of a line are compared at one resolution: when either end's crossing walk does not finish, both sizes on that line come from runs, and the other line keeps its crossings. The frame predicts where to look but samples only as the last grid. Used first where nothing anchors the corner, it lost flat anti-aliased renders at 1.25-1.3 px/module, where sizes 1-2 % off read as perspective.

- The stages in front of the frame, not the frame, were the limit. With true sizes the frame predicts the alignment pattern within 0.15 module at every version, and at 40-50 % keystone, given the true dimension, the anchored grid of every render whose finders were right lay within 0.16 module of the drawn one. When the frame shipped, every render still failing at 20-30 % keystone and 3-6 px/module either had no three finders found or had a false candidate in the chosen triple, and each read through its true geometry. At 40-50 %, five more had the drawn finders and the wrong dimension. The stages were then counted one at a time (the full sweep's candidates against the drawn finders, the triple chosen, the dimension, and the grid at the true dimension), and each repair went to the stage the counts pointed to: the column's window, the rising diagonal, the dimension from each line, the alternative triples and the corner from the timing patterns, above.

### Piecewise mesh (version 7+)

- The piecewise mesh must not trust any single upstream estimate. Every naive seeding strategy failed measurably before the shipped design was found:

  - (a) Predicting all lattice nodes through the global transform fails when the mesh is needed, because its fourth anchor has the parallelogram error (≈ 2·keystone-shrink, ~9 modules at v20/4%).
  - (b) A finder-only affine seed drifts up to ~1.5 modules mid-edge, because projective foreshortening makes lattice spacing non-uniform.
  - (c) Linear extrapolation of the prediction-only edge nodes fails for the same reason: lattice points are collinear, but their spacing along the line is projective (measured 12 px off where quadratic Lagrange left 1 px).
  - (d) Wide search windows turn data-area false positives into cascading mesh corruption, because the wavefront passes every accepted node on into later predictions.

  The shipped design combines wavefront parallelogram prediction from processed neighbors, tight (2.5-module) windows with a wider window only for starters, iterated homography refinement anchored on the farthest detected node, quadratic edge extrapolation, and the single transform, always tried as well, so the mesh never reads less than that transform.

- A plane in perspective is one projective map, so an anchored transform reads every flat symbol the mesh reads. Over the keystone envelope (versions 14 to 40, 20 payloads a version, 540 renders a cell), the sweep (54,400 renders) and the real images, no read changed with the mesh switched off. Inside the envelope the mesh read 3,647 of 6,480 renders, and the anchored transform read each of them at the same attempt with corners as close or closer. In most cells at 3 to 6 px/module it needed no corrections, where the mesh needed up to 696.
- The mesh is needed where no one transform fits. With the bottom-right alignment pattern painted over, only the mesh read 398 of those 6,480 renders (401 with only its centre module flipped), and on the renders it read, its corners were a median 0.01 to 0.13 module off per cell, against 0.32 to 0.50 through the grid that reads without it (0.57 against 2.02 at worst). On a symbol bowed off the plane, its rows sagging 1 to 4 modules at the middle (versions 14 to 40, 2.2 to 5 px/module, 525 renders), nothing else read any of the 519 that read. At a sag of 0.5 to 0.75 module, nothing else read 101 of 210. A painted-over pattern can still anchor the transform on another mark: 70 of 525 such renders read only through the mesh after it.
- So the anchor decides the order. The mesh comes first only when the alignment search found nothing. Otherwise it runs after the anchored transform and its coverage re-read. Every read stayed the same on every set above. Over the 9,720 intact envelope renders the mesh grid was decoded 12 times instead of 4,515, and a sample of them decoded in 0.88 of the time. End to end, the benchmark's version 25 in perspective and turned version 40 took 0.89 to 0.93, its blurred and fractional version 40 0.96 to 0.98, and the rest 1.00. Lost-alignment renders took 1.01. Putting the mesh after the transform unconditionally also keeps the reads, but then a nearly flat symbol with its pattern lost reads through the parallelogram first, its far corner past half a module on 104 of 525 renders, and lost-alignment decodes took 1.13. This was measured on 2026-09-27 by switching grids off in a probe build.

- Versions 7 to 13 bend too, and their lattice is too small for the large one's rules. Bowed as the tests draw it (rows sagging 0.5 to 3 modules at the middle), versions 14-20 read 640 of 700 through their mesh, while versions 7-13, with no mesh, read 191 of 1,400, all with sags under 1.5 modules. zxing-cpp read 1,393. A 3 × 3 lattice has two interior nodes per line, too few to extrapolate an edge line through, and four nodes give a wavefront nothing to pass on. So each interior node is searched where the finders' frame puts it, and the plane that best fits the three finder centres and the found nodes places the rest (the coordinate-6 row and column, and any interior node not found). The mesh is kept when half the searched nodes are found, and it runs where the large one does.

  Versions 7-13 now read 551 and 561 of 1,400 on two seeds, binarized ones 118 → 512, and the photograph `qrcode-3/22` reads at every right angle. A version 10 whose bottom-right alignment pattern is painted over, which had fallen back to the parallelogram, reads through the mesh with its far corner 0.07 module off. Nothing was lost on the sweep (54,400), the envelope (24,000), the corpus or these sets.

  Each node is searched in a tight window first, then a wider one. The tight window alone misses the nodes a 3.5-module sag moves out of it (545 of the 551). The wide window alone reads fewer dots drawn off their module centres (777 of the 783 in 900, and on one it finds none of the four nodes the tight window finds) and fewer binarized bows (509 of 512). The remaining failures are bows past 1.5 modules, 26 of 841: the plane puts the edge nodes flat where the arc is steepest, while the larger lattices extrapolate them along it. Placed after the parallelogram when nothing anchored, the small mesh read the same, which is why it runs where the large one does. Below version 7 there is no mesh, and bowed versions 2 to 6 read 196 of 700.

  It slows failures. Failing damaged versions 7 to 13 take 2 to 6 % longer, and because it also runs when a wrong dimension of 45 to 69 is retried, two failing photographs (`qrcode-3/03`, `high-res-1`) take about 10 % longer. An anchor found by correlating the 5 × 5 pattern around the frame's prediction read 2 of 7 photograph turns tried, so it is not a lever (measured 2026-09-28).

- A curled large symbol fails at its edge, so the edge is where to measure next. The corpus's `high-res-1` is a version 34 on curled paper at 2.2 px/module, and its mesh keeps 13 to 24 of 25 nodes. At 0° the interior cells read no function module wrong, while the bands along the extrapolated coordinate-6 row and column read about half of theirs wrong, and searching those edge nodes where the mesh puts them still fails. Only the version read beside a finder names version 34: the decoder samples 145 and 149 and drops the version the 149 grid names, and 153 fails too. The lead is to trace the edge along the alignment patterns on the timing lines, as rMQR traces its perimeter, with the dimension from that finder-local read. The same trace is the lead for bows past 1.5 modules at versions 7 to 13.

### Matrix and format decoding

- A mirrored matrix does not reliably fail at the format stage. The transposed format bit sequence can land within BCH correction distance of a different valid format pattern, so a mirrored image can surface as `DataUncorrectable` (the wrong mask garbles everything downstream) instead of `FormatInformationInvalid`. The mirror retry (transpose + re-decode) must therefore trigger on any failure, not just format errors.
- Testing "corrupted format info" needs care for the same reason. Flipping all 15 format bits gives the complement, which may be close to another valid codeword, so the negative test searches for a pattern with distance > 3 from all 32 candidates instead of assuming any corruption is rejected.
- A rule enforced by one conditional needs a test that fails without it. The Structured Append header is attached only on `Success` and needs 16 bits after its mode indicator. Deleting the first conditional, or loosening the guard to 15 bits, left the whole suite green: the stream tests called the bit-stream decoder directly, every fixture decoded, and the seeded fuzz test reached the header only with a multiple of four bits left. Every matrix fixture is now also decoded into a one-character destination and must come back without the header, and four hand-built streams sit at 15 to 18 remaining bits. A fixed seed covers only the branches it happens to reach, so boundaries are written by hand.
- The RS decoder's convention must be read off the encoder, not assumed. QR uses generator roots α^0..α^(n-1) (b = 0), which puts an X_k factor in the Forney formula that b = 1 conventions omit. Deriving it from `EccBinaryEncoder`'s documented generator polynomial made the round trip pass on the first run.

### Performance

End-to-end numbers are in `src/FeatherQR.Benchmark`. `QRCodeDecodeEndToEnd` covers the matrix (scenarios mirroring the encode ones), correctable damage and a version 6 image. `QRCodeImageDecodeEndToEnd` covers large and no-symbol images, with a fractional pitch, a rotation and a soft render beside the hard ones, because a shape at a whole number of pixels per module measures an alignment as much as a stage. Every change to the shared threshold and finder scan is also measured on the Micro QR and rMQR image classes.

- Codeword extraction was 78 % of a large matrix decode, and the benchmark had misattributed it. A stage profile of `TryDecode(QRCodeData)` at versions 39 and 40 (x64, 2026-09-20) gave extraction 115 to 140 µs of 150 to 178, the bit stream reader 28 to 36, and everything else under 5 %. The per-module walk paid a blocked-bit test, a stream-end test, a data-dependent branch and a memory OR per module (3.8 ns a module at mask 0), and the mask predicate on top made the cost depend on the mask: 114 µs at mask 0, 147 to 154 at masks 5 to 7. `QRCodeStructuredAppendDecode` showed that as a 1.26x "header cost", because its two arms re-encode the content and are free to pick different masks. Two arms are comparable only when the stage under them does not depend on something they choose differently. With the run walk the ratio is 1.00 on every shape. End to end, a version 40 symbol went 170 → 43 µs, and version 10 15 → 4.4 µs.
- Two expected wins in that kernel measured nothing, and one expected loss was real. Replacing the per-run division with a reciprocal multiply was inside the noise, so the division stayed. The bounds-checked form of the walk measured about 28 % slower, so the unchecked one shipped behind two entry checks (mask pattern in range, matrix at least size²). The unpack in front of it (`QRCodeData.GetCoreData`, 3.8 µs) looked like a stage worth designing around, until it turned out to be one call away from the encoder's vector bit expansion, which writes the same layout in 0.4 µs. Check whether a stage is slow or just unoptimized before removing it.
- The bit stream reader took one bit per call, and after the extraction change it was two thirds of a large decode. `BitReader.Reads` looped over a bounds-checked single-bit read, about 1.2 ns a bit. It now takes a field out of a 64-bit window (one big-endian load, two shifts. The last seven bytes of a stream are assembled bytewise). A Byte segment is read in one call, a copy when the payload is byte aligned and a shift of eight bytes a step otherwise. On net8.0 and later the Byte segment's text is one pass of the framework's transcoder, which checks validity as it writes, replacing a hand-written validator followed by a count and a transcode. The version 40 bit stream stage on x64 went Byte 27.8 → 0.1 µs, UTF-8 behind an ECI 28.4 → 1.8, mixed 36.2 → 2.0, Numeric 31.3 → 7.0, and end to end 43 → 15 to 22 µs a symbol (4.4 → 1.7 at version 10). The reader is shared, so Micro QR and rMQR decode through it too. A failed read now throws before it consumes anything, where the bit loop first consumed what was left.
- One transcoder pass has to answer "too small" before it knows whether the text is valid. Undeclared bytes are UTF-8 only if every sequence is well formed, and ISO-8859-1 otherwise, and a one-pass transcoder meets a short destination before it has seen the rest. Reporting `DestinationTooSmall` is safe either way: UTF-16 units never outnumber UTF-8 bytes, substitutions included, so a destination too small for the UTF-8 reading is too small for the char-per-byte one. The same fact makes the explicit return an equivalent mutant of falling through to the ISO-8859-1 size check. It stays so a reader need not know the inequality to see that UTF-8 text is never widened. The Shift_JIS guess narrowed it: a Shift_JIS reading needs a character a pair, fewer than its bytes, so the early answer is given only for a segment that is valid UTF-8 or that the guess rules out, and a guessed segment is counted by its own reading. The strict validator stays for the older targets and for the Micro QR generator's mirror of this rule. `ByteSegmentCharsetParityTest` checks both implementations and the mirror against an oracle that uses neither.
- Two loop rewrites of the numeric and alphanumeric payloads measured nothing or worse, and a third was not worth its path. Keeping the output index in a local and dropping the per-group bit check (the payload check above the loop already covers it) left Numeric at 7.0 µs and slowed the mixed shape from 2.0 to 3.7 µs, because a slice per segment costs more on a plan's short runs than the local saves on a long one. Five 10-bit groups per window load were estimated at 7 → 4.8 µs, about 10 % of a pure-numeric version 40 decode, at the price of a second decode path and a peek API in the shared decoder, and were deferred. After this phase extraction is the largest stage again (about 11 of 15 µs on Byte).
- With the mask and the reader fixed, the Structured Append ratio shows alignment. A version 10+ set symbol's header (20 + 4 + 16 bits) leaves its Byte payload byte aligned and the plain symbol's (4 + 16) does not, so the set takes 0.94 of the plain symbol's time. Behind a 12-bit ECI header it is the other way round, 1.05. Both are the copy against the shift in `ReadBytes`, under 1 µs.
- Damage on a large symbol shows end to end only when it reaches most blocks. A clean symbol exits after its syndromes, so `QR_*_Corrected_Decode` flips modules and keeps a draw only when the decoder reports exactly that many corrected errors, because a flip on a function pattern carries no codeword. Version 1-L with 2 errors went 302 → 526 ns. Version 40-H with 6 errors measured the same as clean (21.65 and 21.63 µs), since at least 75 of its 81 blocks stayed clean and the corrections were inside the run-to-run noise. With 81 errors, about one a block, it went 21.66 → 38.68 µs (x64, 2026-10-02).
- For a large symbol the image path is 25x the matrix decode, and its largest stage is the histogram. The same x64 measurement (2026-09-21, hard-edged synthetic renders at 3, 4 and 8 px/module, one decode attempt) gave Otsu 120 to 220 µs, finder search 65 to 150, dimension estimate plus mesh plus sampling 120 to 180, and matrix decode 14.5. The Otsu figure does not rise steadily with the pixel count (184 µs for 555² against 122 for 740²), because the fill's uniform-group fold needs eight equal pixels in a row, which 3 px/module almost never gives. So the most common module sizes take the per-pixel path, on the two-valued input that path handles worst. That lead shipped. See the histogram entry below.
- A short kernel can finish measuring before the JIT has promoted it. With warmup by iteration count, the first shape of a process measured 2x to 8x slow for the fast kernels but correctly for the 100 µs reference. Warming up by time removed the error.

- The syndrome pass dominates steady-state cost. Every decode pays it (clean blocks exit early after it), and Berlekamp-Massey/Chien/Forney run only on blocks that contain errors. A GFNI kernel (net10.0+ x64, `EccBinaryDecoder.X86.cs`) measured ~284× per version-40 block, and end-to-end version-40 matrix decode dropped 369 µs → 131 µs, so decode is now faster than encode. An AdvSimd kernel (net8.0+ ARM64, `EccBinaryDecoder.Arm64.cs`, 2026-08-20) closes the same gap on ARM: 61× per version-40 block, and Standard QR v1 matrix decode 1,586 → 1,103 ns on Apple M2.

  The ARM kernel is not a port of the GFNI design. GF2P8MULB is hardwired to the AES polynomial, so the x64 design is built around a field isomorphism that lets it borrow that instruction. PMULL has no fixed modulus, so ARM pays for the reduction mod 0x11D (by nibble-split table lookup) and reads the per-byte data terms from 24 KB of lazily built tables. The same round improved the scalar tier, which netstandard2.0/2.1 runs, to four syndromes per pass (2.2-2.9× on large blocks).

  Every build without the 256-bit GFNI tier runs a 128-bit kernel (`EccBinaryDecoder.Vector128.cs`, 2026-10-01): x64 without AVX, x64 on a CPU without GFNI, .NET 8 on x64 (GFNI is a .NET 10 API, so .NET 8 ran the scalar pass even with AVX2), and WebAssembly. It is the AdvSimd kernel's structure on portable vectors, and does the multiply that `PMULL` does, by each lane's constant K (a fixed power of α), through linearity. a·K is the XOR of K·x^b over the set bits b of a, so a multiply is eight rounds of a sign-bit mask, an AND with a plane of K·x^b and an XOR, from 768 bytes of planes and with no reduction. It runs the pass in 0.06 to 0.18 of the scalar time on a default NativeAOT publish, 0.06 to 0.23 on WebAssembly AOT and 0.14 to 0.36 interpreted (148-, 45- and 24-byte blocks). Version 40 matrix decode takes 0.21, 0.25 to 0.32 and 0.33 of its time before. Berlekamp-Massey/Chien/Forney stay scalar on every target.

- The ARM syndrome kernel was bound by its carried chain, and the fix was re-association, not a split. With a four-byte Horner step, the AdvSimd kernel's chain (acc → PMULL → UZP → TBL → EOR, about 14 cycles a step on Apple M2) was the whole cost: Reed-Solomon took 5.4 µs of a 19.6 µs version 40 decode there, against 1.7 of 15 on x64 behind GFNI, and halving the vector work had gained only 20 %. An earlier attempt, never shipped, split the accumulator chain four ways across the codeword. It measured −21.5 % at 149 codewords but lost at rMQR sizes (no rMQR block exceeds 68 codewords), because a split's combine multiplier depends on the block length and its fixed cost does not shrink with the block.

  Re-associating Horner instead takes eight bytes a step: the multiply that joins two four-byte data terms depends on data alone, so it falls off the chain. This form has no length-dependent term and won at every block shape the three symbologies use, measured through `TryCorrect` on the M2 (2026-09-21):

  - 0.53x to 0.54x at version 40's 145- to 153-byte blocks.
  - 0.75x to 0.83x over rMQR's 25- to 68-byte blocks (54 shapes, 0.45x to 0.98x).
  - 0.76x to 0.81x at Micro QR M3 and M4, level at M2, and 1.07x (5 ns) at M1's five-byte block.
  - On the syndrome pass alone, 0.44x at 148 bytes and 0.59x at 45.

  The sixteen-byte tree tied at 148 and lost 10 % at 45, because from eight bytes on the loop is throughput-bound (about 100 instructions a step). Two throughput hypotheses were refuted in the same round (immediate-offset row pairing lost 10 %, pre-split multiplier halves tied), and work on the loop stopped there. Version 40 Byte matrix decode went 19.5 → 16.7 µs on the `QRCodeData` entry and 19.1 → 16.2 on the span entry. Version 10 went 2.07 → 1.84 and version 1 0.28 → 0.26. The kernel is still shared by all three symbologies.

- A flat ns-per-iteration across sizes means one kernel is the whole cost. Before the AdvSimd tier, ARM matrix decode ran at a constant 3.07-3.15 ns per syndrome inner-loop iteration across a 50x size range, which proved the syndrome pass was nearly all of it. The same item was already under 1 % on x64 after GFNI, so ARM was still at the pre-GFNI position. Re-run that ratio before assuming a component still dominates.
- The syndrome destination is 32 bytes wide, not `eccCount`. Every vector tier keeps every syndrome in lanes and stores whole registers, so `ComputeSyndromes` requires an `EccBinaryDecoder.SyndromeLanes`-length span regardless of the ECC count, and lanes past `eccCount` hold meaningless syndromes of unused roots. This is a caller contract across symbologies. A caller sizing the span to `eccCount` throws on x64 (the GFNI store is bounds-checked) but silently corrupts memory on ARM64, so x64 CI cannot catch the ARM failure mode. Each kernel has a test of its own store width (`GfniKernel_WritesExactlySyndromeLanes`, `AdvSimdKernel_WritesExactlySyndromeLanes`, `Vector128Kernel_WritesExactlySyndromeLanes`).
- The isomorphism root matters. β = 0x03 makes φ its own inverse, so one matrix constant serves both directions. Unrolling beyond ×4 stalls, because the loop moves from latency-bound (accumulator chain) to bound by GFNI-port throughput. Pre-mapping the whole codeword to remove the in-loop affine measured slower: that affine was off the carried dependency chain, so removing it saved nothing, while the extra pass cost real time.
- The large symbols had stopped using the sampler that was vectorized for them. Version 14 and up then sampled through the piecewise mesh first, and that loop had stayed scalar: a cell walk, a division, two lerps and a scattered load per module, 94 to 137 µs at version 40, half of a clean 3 px image decode once the threshold was fast. It became cheap through where things are computed, not only through vector width. The cell a column falls in and the fraction across it are the same for every row, so they go in a table once a call and the division leaves the module loop (0.78 on its own. This step is portable, and it is what the netstandard builds run. Every .NET build class has had a vector tier since, below). A cell's start and span are taken once a row, and an 8-module vector step is built from them by broadcast. Only the steps that straddle two cells need a select, and the version alone decides which those are. Version 40 sampling went 114 → 19 µs, version 20 33 → 6.3, and 135 → 28 on a 3.5 MB rotated image where the loads were expected to be the limit. It is now cheaper than the global transform's vector rows on the same grid, which cannot hoist their division out of the loop.
- A sampler is right only when it picks the same pixel, and three things decided that. The multiply and the add stay separate, because fused they can differ by an ulp and truncate into the next pixel. The float-to-int conversion has to match the reference's, whose cast differed by runtime: before .NET 9 it was the raw x64 conversion (INT_MIN for NaN and for anything out of range, 0 after the clamp), from .NET 9 it saturates, and on WebAssembly it differs again between interpreted and AOT-compiled code. The tier at first had a form for each .NET, found only because the parity test runs on net8.0 as well as net10.0. The kernel search had run on one. Since the 128-bit tier (2026-09-30), the reference takes each coordinate through `PixelIndex.Clamp`, which clamps to the far edge before the conversion and gives the same pixel on every runtime, and every tier has one form. The upper clamp is a float minimum with the limit as the first operand, so a NaN lane passes through, converts to INT_MIN and becomes 0 at the integer maximum, where the reference puts it. The other operand order turns NaN into the far edge of the image. None of these show on a symbol inside its image with finite nodes, so the test scenes are built from what can go wrong: every mesh version, bent meshes, nodes off their predictions, symbols pushed past all four image edges, and nodes that are NaN, infinite or past int range.
- Several variants were refuted on the way, each for a reason worth keeping.
  - Spreading a start and a span to all 177 columns every row, to get the cell index out of the loop, cost more in stores than the indirection it removed (77 → 102 µs). The first vector form built on it measured 0.72 and nearly closed the question, because a variant whose parent was refuted also measures the parent's cost.
  - Branchless clamps gained nothing, since a symbol inside its image never takes those branches.
  - An AVX2 gather lost 9 % to eight scalar loads, and would have read past the last pixel.
  - Removing a register spill by interleaving the per-cell arrays lost 5 to 10 %: a spill that is one load is not worth a more expensive address.
  - Two mutants survived the first planted-fault run, and both were the tests' fault: a y clamp against the x limit (every test image was square), and `<` for `<=` on the threshold (every pixel was 0 or 255). The scenes are now non-square, with pixels on either side of the threshold.
- Perspective sampling SIMD helps only large symbols. An AVX2 kernel (net8.0+) achieved 2.7× at version 40 (79 µs → 29 µs), with a scalar row-hoisted fallback elsewhere. The loop is not division-bound: module computations are independent, so out-of-order execution hides division latency (halving the division count measured no gain), and the cost was scalar conversion, clamp and branch overhead. Sampling is ~0.8% of a typical (version 4) image decode, so the win matters for large symbols only. The overhead finding transfers to 128-bit lanes. A Vector128 kernel (two independent 4-lane chains per iteration plus a 4-lane cleanup tail, with exactly the scalar op sequence so lanes stay bit-identical) gave Apple M2 1.84–1.93× across versions 4–40. The two-chain unroll and the cleanup tail are each worth only 2–5%, which confirms fdiv latency is mostly hidden even at 128 bits and the win comes from amortizing fixed per-iteration work. frecpe reciprocal estimate and FMA are excluded by contract, not cost: both break the SIMD-equals-scalar byte identity that keeps the fallback testable.
- Alignment search cost is dominated by the failure path. The expanding window sweep (4→8→16 modules) runs to completion when no pattern exists, up to 4× per failed decode (secondary dimension × inversion), and was a baseline ~40% of an image decode. An AVX2 kernel (32-px SIMD dark-mask classification + tzcnt run walk × a ⌊moduleSize/2⌋ row stride) achieved 23× on the not-found sweep. The vertical cross-check recenters exactly, so striding gives identical results. The finder scan's walk-vs-build split (below) transfers intact to this kernel's much shorter windows (65–257 px vs full rows): the same NEON 64-px fold + portable 16-px tier gave Apple M2 1.4× at the prediction, 3.8× at 3 modules off and 5.8× on the not-found sweep. The same caveat applies: the walk restructure alone slows the happy path, because a single ~65 px row scan is too short to repay the mask setup without the vector classify. Successful-decode E2E is unmoved (alignment is <1% of `Image_Url_M`). The gain lands on failed decodes of non-QR input.
- Finder scan striding must be envelope-safe, not based on module size. The finder scan reuses the SIMD mask-walk kernel shape, but its row stride cannot come from the module size, which is unknown before detection, so the bound comes from the worst case. The 1:1:3:1:1 band is 3 modules tall for an axis-aligned symbol. (Under rotation the surviving band narrows: the rMQR follow-up measured a floor of 5 rows at 3 px/module, which is why `TryFind` relies on its complementary pass rather than on this arithmetic.) A version-40 symbol filling the frame has the smallest possible modules, so stride 3·height/(4·177) still hits every supported symbol's band several times. A failed stride pass rescans only the skipped rows, keeping its candidates. The union covers exactly the rows of a full scan for one sweep of total work, so detection can never regress (a naive full-rescan fallback measured 0.87×, a regression, in the scalar variant). The best-3 selection before that fallback must run on a copy, because it compacts and sorts the candidate list in place. Together these gave 9.6–11.4× on the scan, and image E2E (`Image_Url_M`) 309 µs → 132 µs (−57%). The SIMD walk alone is bit-identical to the scalar walk and parity-tested.
- The finder scan's SIMD split is walk-vs-build, and only the build is per-ISA. The tzcnt run walk is platform-neutral, and the ~15-line dark-bitmask build is the only ISA-specific piece (AVX2 vpmovmskb / NEON / portable 128-bit `ExtractMostSignificantBits`, gated on `Vector128.IsHardwareAccelerated`, since Vector256 acceleration implies it). NEON has no movemask. Folding 64 pixels into one mask word (4 unsigned compares AND per-byte bit weights + 3 pairwise adds, the simdjson bulk-movemask shape) beat per-16 `ExtractMostSignificantBits` by 8–11% and the scalar walk by 3.3–4.1× on Apple M2. The walk restructure alone (scalar mask build) gave only 1.1–1.4×, so the win comes from the vector classify. Byte-lane `Vector128.LessThan` is already an unsigned compare (cmhi), so the x64 `min(v, t−1) == v` trick is unnecessary on the 128-bit path. Image E2E (`Image_Url_M`, M2) went 129 µs → 76 µs (−41%).

- On a large symbol the finder search is mostly refused cross-checks, and their walk paid for its generality. Once the threshold and the mesh sampler were vector code, the search was 56 to 66 % of a rendered version 40 decode. Such a symbol has 7,800 to 12,200 dark runs on the strided rows, where 280 to 800 windows pass the row's 1:1:3:1:1 check, 6 to 9 % of those pass the column's, and 6 to 21 become candidates. Every other one is a data module, refused after a walk of 30 to 90 pixels that chose its axis per pixel, read each pixel through a checked two-dimensional index, and counted its runs in a stack buffer.

  `FinderPatternFinder.MeasureRuns` is one walk for the column, the row and the diagonal. The distance between two pixels of the line and the pixels on each side of the centre are worked out once, the loops count down, and no reference is formed outside the image. The pixels read, their order and the verdict on the runs are unchanged. The loops it replaced are its reference, run by `TryFindScalar`. `FinderRunWalkParityTest` compares the runs themselves, from every pixel of non-square images, because on most centres the verdict is a refusal whatever the runs were.

  On x64 the finder search took 0.83 to 0.92 of its time on rendered symbols (version 40 at 4 px/module 110 → 97 µs, at 8 px 158 → 140), 0.84 to 0.95 photo-like and 0.89 to 0.99 rotated, and was level on noise, where a walk is 11 pixels long and most windows never reach one. Image decode took 0.83 to 0.95 on rendered symbols, 0.89 to 0.98 photo-like and 0.94 to 1.00 rotated, with the no-symbol inputs level. Fewer than one hit in ten reaches the row or the diagonal walk, so nearly all of that gain is the column's.

- The prototype promised 0.37 to 0.52 on that walk and the search got about two thirds of it, for the reason the histogram benchmark had already shown. Both arms of the prototype were functions of eight and nine arguments, while the shipped loops had been inline in the cross-check and paid no call, so the copy standing in for them was slower than the code it stood for, and the new walk had to pay for a call the old one never made. As a plain call it was level, to within 2 %, with inlining it into its two callers. The inlined form was ahead on most rows and is the one kept. The same run showed how little one reading is worth here: four passes of one binary on one input spread from 56 to 66 µs, and a gradient with no cross-check at all read 24 against 25.

- A refused cross-check stops walking as soon as it is refused, and the centre run decides that. The false hits on a large symbol are ordinary data: side runs of about two modules around a centre of about three, in a window of about nine. Nothing in them runs long, so tightening the cap on a side run, the original plan, cut the pixels read by 15 %. The accept conditions do give an order:

  - The strict ratio puts three totals below fourteen centres and fourteen side runs below three totals, so a side run is shorter than the centre run.
  - The near-miss ratio ties a side run to a third of the centre.
  - The total is inside its window (within 40 % of the row for the row again, 5/12 to 12/5 of it for the column, see the finder in perspective above) and below fourteen thirds of the centre.

  `FinderPatternFinder.MeasureRunsBounded` therefore measures the centre run first, in both directions. It gives up the walk at the first run that exceeds what is left of those budgets, and an empty side run is a refusal too. A cross section with a centre of one module is refused once its first side run reaches one module. The small crisp runs of the whole-pattern check lie inside the same bounds, so both modes of the axis cross-checks use it. The diagonal has no expected total and walks as before. Pixels read per hit fell to 0.55 to 0.60 on a symbol and 0.67 on noise.

  Exactness is a property of the verdict alone: no run vector outside a bound may be accepted. So `FinderRunBoundsTest` checks `AxisRunBounds` against the ratio checks themselves, over every vector for expected totals up to 40, four hundred thousand more at the tolerance edges up to 400 px/module, and every centre of every total of the window up to 200. The last set is needed because vectors drawn around the nominal shape never land on the corners of the total window, where a bound one step too tight refuses a cross section the verdict accepts. `FinderCrossCheckParityTest` compares the cross-check through both walks bit for bit, grey second look included.

  Both tests were sized against hand-planted faults, every term of the bounds and the walk tightened by one. Ten times as many draws at the tolerance edges caught no fault that 400,000 miss, except three that the exhaustive or the window-corner walk catches, and a second seed of the crisp scenes caught nothing the first misses. Six tightenings survive both tests at their full sizes, and none is a fault the tests miss:

  - Two change no bound (the near-miss floor on the centre is never the lower of the two floors, and the near-miss side cap rounds the same with either constant).
  - One changes only an expected total of 10, which the exhaustive walk covers.
  - Three tighten the like-edge caps where no like-edge cross section reaches them. Summed, the pair and shift conditions keep nineteen side runs at least two below sixteen centres, and three side runs at least two below the total, which every like-edge vector up to twelve modules of 1,200 px bears out.

  Against the unbounded walk (x64, median of six alternating passes), the finder search took 0.91 to 1.01 at version 40 and 3 px/module, 0.81 to 0.86 at 4 px, 0.81 to 0.87 at 8 px, and 0.94 on noise, the first gain of this work on an image with no symbol. With the walk above, against the loops both replaced, it took 0.71 to 0.92 at version 40, image decode 0.78 to 0.98, and no-symbol noise 0.92 to 0.93. A label-sized symbol at 3 and 4 px/module gives a third of the previous gain back (the search 1.03 to 1.06 against the unbounded walk, 0.90 to 0.99 against the old loops), because a fifth of its hits are real finders, walked in full either way, and the bounded walk costs more to enter. Leaving the centre check out did not recover it.

- The row walk was bound by its branches, and a branch-free kernel is worth more inside a decode than on its own. The mask walk judges a window at the end of every dark run with up to fifteen compares, each of which may leave early, and a search judges ten thousand windows on a large symbol and forty-five thousand on an image with no symbol, nearly all refused. With 256-bit vectors or ARM64 AdvSimd, rows of 32 to 4,095 pixels now go to the edge-list kernel (`FinderPatternFinder.RowEdges.cs`). Every 64 pixels become one word, which is never stored, and the word's rising and falling edges fill an array of run starts and one of run ends. Sixteen windows a step (eight on ARM64) are classified without a branch by the same three integer checks (strict ratio, near miss, small crisp runs). Only flagged windows run scalar code, in row order, through the same follow-ups and cross-checks.

  The strict ratio is checked in integers and gives the float form's verdict on every input (they can differ only where total / 7f is inexact, and equality needs a total divisible by 14, where it is exact). Both ratio checks share one difference per run, total − 7·run, written so nothing leaves a sixteen-bit lane, which bounds the row width. Targets with neither instruction set, and wider rows, kept the mask walk. A scalar edge list measured level with it, so the portable tier did not change then (every 128-bit target has taken the kernel since, three entries below). The numbers below are for the x64 tier the kernel was first measured on. ARM64 took the same kernel on 128-bit vectors two entries below.

  The row pass alone on x64 took 0.36 to 0.58 of the mask walk's time on symbols and 0.20 on noise, the ordering unchanged with AVX-512 disabled. In `QRCodeImageDecodeEndToEnd` (span entry, against the walks above), version 40 at 3 px/module went 112 → 85 µs, at 3.4 px 127 → 96, rotated 4 px 421 → 276, soft 4 px 298 → 239, the version 6 URL 10.7 → 9.3, no-symbol noise 2,427 → 1,408, and a gradient stayed level. Allocated was unchanged. In the rotated decode the kernel saved three times what it saved on its own (145 µs against 45), because in isolation the old walk's branches are learnt from one row sequence repeated, and in a decode they are not. That is the 1.4× to 1.7× the phase's profile had measured between the two.

- A row kernel that reports a window too many changes no result, so candidate parity cannot test it. The cross-checks judge the same row again with the scalar checks and refuse what the row stage should not have sent. Twelve of twenty-two planted faults in the kernel survived a test that compared candidate lists bit for bit, and every one over-reports or sits in a stage whose output matters only when accepted. So the kernel's two stages became functions of their own. `ExtractRowEdges` is checked against a pixel-by-pixel scan at every length around the vector and word sizes, and `ClassifyWindows` against the scalar predicates themselves, for every run vector up to 14 pixels and three million at the tolerance edges up to the width limit (`FinderRowEdgesTest`). Three faults still survive, all over-reporting by construction: the near-miss flag kept while the grey levels are off, which sends a window the mask walk never measures to the coverage check, and two follow-ups skipped after a flag.

  One class of over-report is visible to candidate parity, and `FinderRowKernelParityTest`'s scene list has the scene that shows it. A finder flush against the right edge, whose ring is light on one row, leaves that row a window short, and because the edge buffer still holds the row above, a lane read past the last window makes a candidate the scalar walk never makes.

- The edge-list kernel also runs on ARM64, built from what that machine makes cheap. After the histogram tier, on the mask walk, the search was 10 to 50 % of a version 40 decode on an Apple M2 and 46 % of a no-symbol noise image. The kernel above now also takes 128-bit vectors:

  - The row's word comes from the NEON fold the mask walk already used (there is no movemask).
  - Eight windows are classified a step (`ClassifyWindows8`. Sixteen as two halves lost 5 to 30 % on the last step of every row).
  - A step's three verdicts become bits (`LaneBits`: narrow, one weight a lane, add across, since `ExtractMostSignificantBits` is a sequence there) only after one add across their OR says a lane is flagged.
  - A word's rising and falling edges are written by one loop, one of each per iteration, so their two two-cycle bit-clear chains overlap (0.78 to 0.92 of two loops in a row on symbols).

  x64 takes the same loop. Its bit clear is one `blsr`, so there is no chain to overlap, and the extraction alone measured level, but the loop branches half as often, and the whole row pass measured 0.85 to 0.97 of two loops on version 40 symbols and level on noise and on a label-sized symbol. End to end that is inside the noise (±3 %), as expected for a few percent of a stage that is a fifth of the decode. It stays because one form on both machines also puts the ARM64 loop under x64 CI. The windows are judged by the same integer arithmetic throughout, and `FinderRowEdgesTest` and `FinderRowKernelParityTest` run on ARM64 unchanged but for the lane count.

  On the M2 the row pass alone took 0.13 to 0.19 of the mask walk's time on rendered version 40 symbols, 0.25 on a label-sized one and 0.37 on noise, where three quarters of what is left is the coverage measurement on near misses, which every kernel pays. In the image decode stage harness, version 40 at 3 px/module went 270 → 138 µs, 3.4 px 300 → 164, 8 px 441 → 302, 4 px rotated 757 → 550, 4 px soft 520 → 326, no-symbol noise 740 × 740 3,377 → 1,778, and a gradient stayed level. In `QRCodeImageDecodeEndToEnd` (span entry) the figures were 269 → 137, 307 → 161, 756 → 549, 530 → 334, the version 6 URL 15.4 → 11.6, noise 3,308 → 1,723, Micro QR M4 6.3 → 5.9 and rMQR R17x139 34.5 → 25.1. Allocated was unchanged.

  The kernel's gate also found a separate bug, filed apart: `GreyLevels.FromHistogram` computed the light mean in float, and past 2²⁴ in the weighted sum it rounded above 255 and enabled the grey levels on a two-valued image. The scan bounds are now integers (see the grey-levels entry below).

- Every other 128-bit target also takes the edge-list kernel. x64 without AVX (a default NativeAOT publish) and WebAssembly had kept the mask walk. On them the row's word is four 16-byte compares with a movemask each, and the rest is the ARM64 form: eight windows a step, and the OR of the three verdicts becomes bits first, so a step that flags nothing makes bits once. Against the mask walk (version 40 at 3 px/module and 740 × 740 noise), the row pass alone took 0.43 and 0.54 on default NativeAOT, 0.25 and 0.49 on WebAssembly AOT, and 0.28 and 0.47 interpreted. Image decode took 0.58 to 0.96 on default NativeAOT, 0.36 to 0.80 on WebAssembly AOT and 0.38 to 0.94 interpreted, the gain largest on the version 25 keystone and smallest on the rMQR keystone and the bitmap entries. Those builds never run the test suite, so `--parity` checks the kernel's candidates against the scalar walk's on each of them, and on the JIT with AVX off in CI.

- The mesh sampler has an ARM64 tier, and four lanes give half of what eight gave. `SampleGridPiecewiseAdvSimd` is the AVX2 tier's step on 128-bit vectors. It runs two steps a loop body and packs their eight pixels into one word for one compare and one store. The tables are read through hoisted references, and the pixel index takes one integer multiply-add. The float operations are the same, in the reference's order, so it picks the same pixel. Its clamp has one conversion form where the AVX2 tier needed two, because the scalar cast on ARM64 has always been the saturating fcvtzs. For the same reason its row tail keeps the plain cast, where the other tiers' tails use `PixelIndex.Clamp`, which ILC for ARM64 compiled with the limit converted inside the loop.

  Against the column-table tier on Apple M2 it measured 0.46 to 0.51 at versions 14 to 40, upright and rotated, and the search for a faster form ended there: the loop issues eight to nine instructions a module at about four a cycle. Variants that swapped one instruction for another (cell parameters kept as vectors, pixels loaded straight into lanes) measured level, and an index vector stored and reloaded as words lost 20 % to partial store forwarding. The AVX2 tier reaches 0.24 of the same column-table tier on x64. This ISA has no wider form.

  In the M2 image decode stage harness, version 40 at 3 px/module went 141 → 115 µs, 8 px 293 → 266, 4 px rotated 544 → 521, 4 px soft 325 → 304, and version 20 at 3 px 42 → 34. In `QRCodeImageDecodeEndToEnd` (span entry) the figures were 139 → 114, 161 → 137, 545 → 525 and 326 → 303, with the version 6 URL and the no-symbol inputs level. Allocated was unchanged. `SampleGridPiecewiseParityTest` enters the tier where it enters the AVX2 one. Two planted faults survived, and both were examined. One was the minimum's operand order, which `Avx.Min` cares about and `Vector128.Min` does not. The other was in a four-lane leftover loop, since deleted: odd versions leave five modules after the eight-module steps and do enter it, but the scalar tail after it samples the same pixel from the same floats, so no output could tell the two apart.

- Every other 128-bit target also has a mesh tier. x64 without AVX and WebAssembly sampled the mesh through the column table. `SampleGridPiecewiseVector128` is the ARM64 tier's step on portable vectors, taking each coordinate to its pixel through `VectorCast.ToPixel`. The mesh runs only when nothing anchors the grid or the anchored grid fails. On a bowed symbol it was 9.8 % (version 25) and 11.4 % (version 40) of a WebAssembly AOT decode. Against the column table (version 40 at 3 px), the sampler alone took 0.50 on default NativeAOT, 0.30 on WebAssembly AOT and 0.41 interpreted. Bowed decodes at versions 25 and 40, with the histogram's 128-bit tier, took 0.84 and 0.89, 0.72 and 0.76, and 0.92 and 0.93.

- The Otsu histogram never sends a rendered symbol's two values through memory. `histogram[value]++` serializes on store forwarding when consecutive pixels hit the same bin, and a rendered symbol is two values in long runs. The first fix folded eight equal pixels into one `+= 8` (8–10× on the images it was measured on, while the textbook multi-lane fix managed ~2.4×), but those images were 8 px/module in a width that is a multiple of eight, the one layout where every group of eight is uniform. The same two-valued symbol at 8.4 px/module cost 6× as much a pixel, 3 px/module almost never folds, and a smooth gradient, where neighbours share a bin, ran at 1.56 ns a pixel against 0.09.

  The 256-bit tier (net8.0+, `Binarizer.FillHistogramVector256`) compares 32 pixels against 0 and against 255, counts the two masks in registers, and sends only the other pixels to the bins, so a two-valued block costs the same wherever its boundaries fall. A block that is mostly other values goes to the scalar groups, and after two blocks in a row with neither counted value, the next 31 are taken without the test. The x64 threshold stage at version 40 went 274 → 14 µs at 3.4 px/module, 442 → 22 at 4.4 px, 1,209 → 83 at 8.4 px, 193 → 75 in the 8 px aligned best case, 357 → 115 rotated at 4 px and 844 → 249 on a no-symbol gradient. Image decode went 549 → 204, 797 → 241, 1,594 → 392, 463 → 337, 716 → 523 and 1,741 → 555 µs. Every bin is identical on every tier (`OtsuHistogramParityTest`, each tier entered directly), so the threshold and the grey levels are too.

- That tier was 8 to 11 % slower on photo-like images, which an end-to-end A/B found after the kernel benchmark had shown the opposite. The benchmark's baseline was the shipped loop copied verbatim but taking the histogram as a span parameter, where the library's is a `stackalloc int[256]` in the same method. The JIT knows that length and drops the bounds check of every `histogram[(byte)v]`, while the copy paid the check per increment. So the copy was slower than the real code on noise (1.15×) and faster on gradients and two-valued images (0.25× to 0.73×), because the check spaced out same-bin increments. Every "against the shipped code" ratio from it was wrong in one direction or the other. Only the order between candidates held. A faithful copy is one whose disassembly matches, not one whose source does. The repair was the untested stretch above:
  - With the test in front of every block, a photo-like threshold measured +8 to +11 %.
  - With 7 untested blocks, +2 to +3 %.
  - With 31, level (0.97 to 1.03 over two runs, inside the harness's spread).
- These were measured and left out of that kernel.
  - Splitting the dense blocks' increments over 4 or 8 sub-histograms, four ways: a gradient gains 8 to 12 %, and noise and photo-like images lose 5 to 20 % to the extra L1 footprint.
  - A fast path for blocks that are wholly 0 and 255 gained 27 to 35 % on two-valued images and lost 4 to 17 % on resampled ones. It was unstable between runs, because the JIT lays the three paths out differently under each workload's profile, which C# cannot steer.
  - A 512-bit tier halved the 256-bit one's time on two-valued images. It was not shipped, because no CI runner is sure to execute it and it would be the library's only 512-bit tier.
  - In a 128-bit tier at 16 pixels a step, a gradient ran 1.85× slower than the scalar walk, with a dense path whose disassembly matched the 256-bit tier's instruction for instruction. Only keeping the 32-pixel cadence (two loads, paired masks) fixed that, and it was still 8 % behind on gradients. It would run on ARM64 and WASM, where the mask extraction costs something else entirely. ARM64 has had its own tier since (two entries below), and x64 without AVX and WebAssembly have run it since 2026-09-30, measured on those builds (below).
  - The scalar tier is the old walk through unchecked references: level on photo-like input, 0.24× to 0.72× on gradients and on resampled and unaligned two-valued images, 1.04× on the aligned best case. These are all x64 figures, for a tier x64 does not run. On ARM64 it measured 0.99 to 1.01 of the loop before it on every input.
- Where no other histogram tier runs, the 128-bit one does. x64 without AVX (a default NativeAOT publish) and WebAssembly counted in scalar. They now run the 256-bit tier's 32-pixel blocks on two 128-bit loads, with a movemask for each compare (`Binarizer.Vector128.cs`). The x64 JIT result above did not carry over. Against the scalar tier, the histogram alone on default NativeAOT, WebAssembly AOT and interpreted took 0.11, 0.09 and 0.16 on rendered version 40 at 3 px, 0.48, 0.31 and 0.51 rotated at 4 px, 0.93, 1.11 and 0.99 on a gradient, and 0.99 to 1.01 soft and on noise, except WebAssembly AOT at 1.04 and 1.07. Image decode, each shape in its own process, took 0.57, 0.60 and 0.79 at version 40 and 3 px, 0.99, 1.02 and 1.01 soft, and 1.01, 1.02 and 1.00 on the no-symbol gradient, inside each run's spread. WebAssembly keeps the tier for that. Moving the dense blocks' group walk out of the vector method lost: a call per dense block cost noise 24 to 35 %, and a call per untested stretch cost soft and noise 9 to 10 %.

- ARM64 has its own histogram tier, built from what that core makes cheap. On an Apple M2 the scalar tier cost twice x64's per pixel wherever increments to one bin chain (1.47 ns on a 3 px render, 2.0 on a gradient), and the same on noise (0.31), which made the threshold 30 to 87 % of a version 40 image decode and the largest stage on every input. `Binarizer.FillHistogramAdvSimd` (net8.0+, `AdvSimd.Arm64`) keeps the 256-bit tier's blocks, on two 128-bit loads, and differs where ARM64 differs:

  - There is no movemask, and `ExtractMostSignificantBits` is a sequence here, four a block. A block's extremes are counted by one add across its two compare masks (each lane is 0, −1 or −2, so the byte sum is minus the count). The zeros accumulate in byte counters drained every 120 blocks. A mask of the other pixels, one bit a byte from a narrowing shift of the compare masked to 0x11, is built only for a sparse block that has any. The general-register popcount is a round trip through the vector unit on this core, and a block that is all 0 and 255 now takes none of these steps.
  - The dense blocks and the untested stretch count into four sub-histograms, pixel i of a group into lane i % 4. x64 refused this for its L1 footprint, but this core's 128 KB L1 holds it: lanes alone took a gradient to 0.22 and photo-like images to 0.82 of the scalar tier. Each lane is its own reference. Addressing lane k as one base plus 256·k made the JIT sign-extend the sum on the way to every load, and cost noise 14 %.
  - The lanes are rented from `ArrayPool` once a call: 4 KB is past the few hundred bytes the library allows on the stack.

  These were measured and refused: two and eight lanes (noise 1.14 at eight), a dense cut-over of 8 or 16 instead of 12, and the sparse walk spread over two lanes.

  The rental, a stack buffer and a 1.5 KB `ushort` form differed by 2 to 10 % in isolation, and by as much on inputs that never touch the lanes, so the difference was not the storage. The decode A/B below cleared the rental. The cause came out later (2026-09-23). The walk sits in its own method so the rental's try region does not reach the block loop, and under dynamic PGO the Tier1 caller inlined it back (4,168 bytes of code with the vector loop in it, against a call without PGO). Measured alone, that took noise to 1.33 and a soft render to 1.11 of the scalar tier. Switching PGO off, or giving the walk the same rental from another caller, put both back to 0.99 and 0.84. Inside a decode the caller is not profiled the same way, and the end-to-end numbers were level either way. The walk is marked `NoInlining`, because a method split meant to keep a loop out of a try region holds only if the JIT cannot undo it, and a FullOpts disassembly does not show what Tier1 does.

  Inside a decode on the M2 at version 40, the threshold stage went 455 → 14 µs at 3 px/module, 559 → 18 at 3.4 px, 2,110 → 103 at 8.4 px, 465 → 93 on the 8 px aligned render and 704 → 335 rotated at 4 px, took 0.79 to 0.88 photo-like, went 1,097 → 243 on a no-symbol gradient, and was level on noise. Image decode (stage harness, median of three alternating passes) took 0.19 to 0.54 at version 40 on rendered symbols, 0.49 to 0.85 rotated and 0.86 to 0.96 photo-like, 0.22 to 0.97 at versions 6 to 20 by the same classes, 1.00 on no-symbol noise, and 0.29 and 0.42 on the gradient. In `QRCodeImageDecodeEndToEnd` (span entry, two runs a side), version 40 at 3 px went 720 → 267 µs, at 3.4 px 859 → 306, rotated 4 px 1,139 → 754, soft 4 px 554 → 525, the version 6 URL 34.1 → 15.4, no-symbol noise 3,304 → 3,318 (level), and the gradient 1,127 → 317. Through the shared threshold, Micro QR M4 went 11.4 → 6.4 µs, rMQR R7x43 12.8 → 7.0 and R17x139 67.6 → 34.7, and rMQR no-symbol noise 8,012 → 7,677 and gradient 145 → 124. Allocated was unchanged, with the span rows at zero. `OtsuHistogramParityTest` enters the tier directly, with inputs long enough to drain the counters many times, and with a call after a noise image that would show lanes left uncleared.

- Whether the grey levels are enabled is a statement about the bins, and it is now made in integers. `GreyLevels.FromHistogram` disables the levels when no pixel lies strictly between the two class means, since every share is then 0 or 1 and says nothing the threshold did not. The scan for such a pixel was bounded by the float means, and a float loses a weighted sum's low bits past 2²⁴, which for a light class at 255 is 65,794 pixels. Past that the mean rounds to 255.00001, the scan reaches bin 255 itself, and whether a pure two-valued image gets the near-miss second look depends on its pixel count: a 555 × 555 render of a version 40 symbol at 3 px/module got it, and the same symbol at 3.4 px did not. A kernel benchmark's gate found this because its scenes reproduced it. The bounds are now the smallest bin above the dark mean and the largest below the light mean, from the integer sums (floor + 1 and ceil − 1), exact at any count. The levels, the scale and the minimum-range check keep their float form.

  `GreyLevelsEnableTest` covers two-valued histograms at seven level pairs and counts from 1 to 4 million, one pixel between at the same counts, the darkness readings and the range check. It also covers the bounds where they are tightest: a pixel in the bin next to either level or next to a class mean that is not a whole number, a class whose count reaches exactly half its weight, and levels exactly the minimum range apart. No decode fixture moved, because on a two-valued image the strict ratio finds the finders and the second look had nothing to add.

- The inverted retry does not count the negative. A pixel of value v is 255 − v in the negative, so the negative's histogram is the first polarity's with bin i at 255 − i. The image decode passes all three image decoders share (`ImageDecodePasses`) count once and, before the retry, reverse the bins in place (`Binarizer.InvertHistogram`). The threshold and the grey levels come from `ComputeOtsuThresholdFromHistogram` either way. The threshold is searched again on the mirrored bins, not mirrored itself, because the search keeps the first of equal splits and two values with nothing between them tie at every split, so on a rendered symbol, exactly that case, `256 − threshold` would be a different threshold. Only an image not read in its first polarity is affected. On x64 a no-symbol gradient went 530 → 287 to 309 µs at 740 × 740 and 1,863 → 1,045 at 1480 × 1480, noise 2,666 → 2,561 and 6,136 → 5,520 (the finder search is the rest), and Micro QR and rMQR on a 400 × 400 gradient 155 → 93. Decodes that succeed are level.
