The existing inverted-decode tests could not see the wiring, because on pure black and white the unmirrored bins give a threshold that also splits the negative. `OtsuInvertedHistogramTest` reads a light-on-dark symbol with modules at 150 on 25 through each decoder and checks the mirrored bins' threshold and grey levels against a per-pixel count of the negative.

- A scan holds one module buffer at a time, or the pool's shared stacks decide whether it allocates.
  - Each grid attempt used to rent its own buffer, so a dimension could have three buffers of one size out at once (the first sampling, another grid compared against it, and a coverage re-read).
  - The array pool keeps one array a size per thread, so the second and third came from per-core stacks every thread shares. With other tests decoding beside it, the failure path allocated 4,120 B in every round, in one of six runs on .NET 8. Alone it never did.
  - Since 2026-09-29 a scan rents one array of three grids for the largest dimension it has sampled (`ModuleWorkspace`), again only for a larger one.
  - `DecodeAllocationTest` checks the peak count of buffers out at once per image (`QRImageDecoder.ModuleBuffersPeak`). Before the change that count was 2 or 3 on the bowed symbol, the next triple and noise.
  - The inverted image's buffer is still out during the negative pass, and a module buffer of the same size bucket then still comes from the shared stacks.
  - The reads measured 0.3 to 1.3 % slower in the fastest of twelve alternating runs (version 6 at 4 px/module, 9.75 to 9.88 µs), the failing images within 0.6 %. Without the counters, and with the workspace renting one grid instead of three, the reads were still 0.5 to 1.0 % slower, so neither is the cause. It was not traced further.
- A workspace passed by `ref` beside spans must not be a `ref struct`. The compiler refuses a `ref ModuleWorkspace` argument next to a stack-allocated span, or next to an `ImageView` built from a local passed by `in` (CS8350), because a ref struct's fields could capture either.
  - The workspace holds only an array and a length, so it is a plain struct.

### Measuring and verifying a hot-path change

These lessons come from the matrix decode round of 2026-09-20 and 21 (codeword extraction, the bit stream reader, the ARM syndrome kernel) and the image round of 2026-09-21 to 23 (the threshold fill, the mesh sampler, the finder search, and their ARM64 tiers). None is about the decoder itself, and each cost a wrong conclusion or nearly did.

- Look for the inverse of an existing table before designing a kernel. Both tables that made extraction fast had been built by the encoder for the opposite direction, and the decoder was already loading them to read one field.
- A cache of something periodic is a table of its period. Asking what the mask bits under one output byte depend on turned a per-version mask stream, 441 KB worst case, into 1,152 bytes for every version.
- Sharing a table with the encoder removes the cross-check a round trip used to give, because both sides would be wrong together. The independent reference walk and the third-party fixtures replace it, and the reference must stay off the shared tables.
- Check parity on a dirty buffer. The reference walk ORs into a cleared buffer and the run walk stores, so a comparison on a buffer of zeros would have passed either way. Comparing on a buffer filled with 0xA5 allowed the clear in `DecodeMatrix` to go.
- An exit criterion is a claim about the format and is checked like one. "Level L and H end the stream in different places" sounded right and tested nothing, because data plus ECC is one total per version. The cut is driven by shortening the output instead.
- A prediction is not a reason. "The smaller footprint will win on ARM64" was written as the reason for a choice, but the measuring machine had less L1 than the target, and the target later reproduced the x64 ordering exactly. The choice rested on memory alone, which needed no second machine.
- A mutation run starts from a baseline that shows the expected count. A TUnit tree filter of the form `/*/*/(A|B)/*` matched no test and still printed `failed: 0`, so twelve planted faults looked like twelve survivors. The baseline line printing `succeeded: 0` gave it away. Run one class per invocation.
- When the red is a missing method, add it in the old style first, because a compile error says nothing about the tests around it. With `ReadBytes` added as a bit loop, the new tests ran against the old reader and split into new contract (seven) and characterization (the rest) by measurement rather than argument.
- An equivalent mutant is a question about the code, not a gap in the tests. The one survivor of the reader round was an explicit return that a later check also covers. It stayed, because seeing that takes an inequality the reader of the code should not need, and the decision is recorded beside the rule it concerns.
- Carry two arms of identical code. On the M2 their spread (0.0 to 1.6 %) made a 24 % gap conclusive, for the cost of one enum value.
- An isolated stage is a hint, and only one call site is real. The bit stream stage measured 7 and then 13 µs from two builds of one harness while the end-to-end figure did not move, and the shipped syndrome kernel measured 94, 148, 198 and 99 ns a block from four call sites. Ratios are compared between candidates on one call site. The quoted figure is the end-to-end A/B, built from an export of the committed tree against the working tree, with the binaries checked to differ.
- A capability-gated test is evidence only on a machine with the capability. `GetCoreData` was routed through a kernel whose AdvSimd parity test had been skipped on every x64 run of two phases. It first executed on the M2, a day after it shipped.
- A second back end changes what is left, not what won. ARM64 reproduced every kernel ordering, but a stage the x64 profile had ruled out of scope at 2 % became the second largest there, at 28 %.
- Open the file before writing the hypothesis. The plan contained a guess about the ARM syndrome kernel that one minute in the source refuted: the kernel's own comment named the real cost.
- Count what a change is meant to reduce before timing it. The run caps were planned on a measurement of 32 pixels walked for a 21 pixel window, taken to mean that walks ran long. Counted per run, the cap as planned saved 15 % and the centre-first walk that replaced it 40 to 45 %, both known before either existed as library code. The count of pixels read does not depend on the machine's load, and at 8 px/module, where every read is a cache line, it is the cost.
- The minimum over passes rewards the luckiest pass. One pass in six of one binary measured 118 µs where the other five measured 163 to 174, and the minimum made that arm look 1.15× better than the arm it lost to in every other pass. Rounds inside a pass share the machine's state. Passes do not. Across alternating passes the figure is the median, and three passes is the fewest that have one.
- Time the stages before the second hypothesis, not after it. The first vector form of the row kernel halved the walk. The two ideas for the rest (the extraction loop's branches, the classification's instruction count) were both wrong, and each took a full benchmark round to find out. Three probes that stop the kernel after each stage then measured 12 % mask, 29 % extraction, 36 % classification and 23 % hit handling. That split showed why a variant that halved the classification had gained nothing (its extraction had grown by as much), and every variant written from it was confirmed.
- Verify a code generation switch in the disassembly. The check that the kernel's ranking holds without AVX-512 first ran with `DOTNET_EnableAVX512F=0`, which .NET 10 ignores (it reads `DOTNET_EnableAVX512=0`). The run reproduced the previous round and would have passed for the answer. Counting mask-register instructions in the exported disassembly, 1,435 and then none, told the two runs apart.
- An isolated stage is a floor, and the sum of floors under-reads the whole. Seven stages of an image decode, each looped alone, summed to 328 µs against a decode of 442 (version 40, 4 px/module, x64), because a stage on its own runs with its part of the image in cache, and in a decode it does not. One arm that runs the stages back to back in one body measured within 3 % of the decode on 33 of 34 inputs. Shares are stated as shares of the decode, and a stage's own figure is a lower bound.
- A benchmark shape at a whole number of pixels per module measures an alignment. The threshold's uniform-group fold was fast only where module boundaries land on multiples of eight pixels, and the same two-valued symbol at 8.4 px/module cost 6x as much a pixel. Every image class now includes a fractional pitch beside the whole ones, and a variant is judged on the fractional, soft and rotated classes first and on the hard renders last.
- Ask the count first. The first question put to the image profile was how many times `SampleAndDecode` runs, and the answer was once on every input. Asking that first justified reading every other column as the cost of a decode rather than of a search. Had the answer been two, it would have ended the round.
- The end-to-end A/B per input class is a detector, not a confirmation. The first histogram tier measured 0.24x to 0.90x on every other class and +8 to +11 % on all nine photo-like inputs, which the kernel benchmark had shown as a win. One class with nine inputs, all of the same sign, separated it from noise, where a single "image decode" number would have averaged it away. The repair took three measured steps, and the first made it worse.
- A surviving mutant that tightens a bound is a statement about the bound. Three faults that lowered the cross-check's centre bound by one survived an exhaustive test of the bound against the verdict, so the derived bound has a pixel of slack. Asking the same question of the formula before the sweep found two terms that could never bind. The derivable bound was kept, at the cost of a pixel.
- A change that gains nothing can be what a gaining change needs. The edge list alone and the integer ratio alone measured level with the row walk, but the branch-free kernel could not be written without either. A variant's verdict is about that variant as an end point, so a series of variants keeps its refuted steps.
- The rows a change cannot reach show whether an end-to-end class can be trusted. One Micro QR run measured its PNG generation rows, identical in both trees, 1.5x slower on the changed side in both passes, and its decode row slower with them. Run again with the order reversed, everything was level. Those rows were looked at only because the decode row looked wrong. Now they are read first.
- A stage probe can miss what the stage does to its neighbours. The edge extraction alone measured level three times, while the row pass it sits in measured 5 to 15 % faster with the one-loop form. The change was one branch per pair of edges, and the classification and flagged-window loops of the same row share the branch predictor with it, so a branch change is judged inside the loop it shares the predictor with.
- A refutation belongs to the machine it was made on. Four sub-histogram lanes were refused four times on x64 for their L1 footprint, and they are the whole gain on gradients and photo-like images on a core with four times the L1. The movemask, the sixteen-window step and the bit extraction of the x64 row kernel each had to be replaced on ARM64, while its structure transferred whole. The record says why a variant lost, because the reason is what may not transfer.
- A warmup that is enough on one machine is not evidence on another. The stage harness's 60 ms had been enough on x64 but left the M2 at Tier0, where a version 40 decode measured 900 µs, and 715 once warmed for 300 ms. A stage figure that moves when the warmup doubles is not valid.
- Restoring a planted fault by moving a backup back keeps the faulted binary. `mv` restores the old timestamp, so the incremental build sees nothing to do. The run after the last fault stayed red until the file was touched. A mutation sweep has not ended until it ends with a rebuilt, counted green baseline.
- Two copies of the benchmark project build none. The benchmark host found a second copy under a worktree in `.claude/` and refused to build, and the first end-to-end pass wrote NA rows without failing its script. Both trees of an A/B are now exported outside the repository, and the script stops on a build refusal.

### Measuring an accuracy change

These lessons come from the rounds measured against other readers (2026-09-21 to 28, all three decoders. The rules are in [qrcode-test-fixtures.md](qrcode-test-fixtures.md#image-decode-sweep)). Each cost a wrong conclusion or nearly did.

- Diagnose stage by stage from the input the decode had. A probe called `EstimateModules` and added the 7 modules the function already counts, giving round, plausible causes (a version or two off for two renders, 8 to 11 modules long for 24 others) that went into the record unchecked. Taken the decoder's way, the two counted within 1.2 modules of the dimension and the 24 within 3.2. A number a probe derives is a claim about the code only once the probe does what the code does.
- Switch each piece off alone on the final code, over every set. Two pieces that were exact in theory changed nothing and were removed (the dimension from each line's sizes, the frame's mesh seeds), and one that looked minor, the timing match through the frame, was worth 47 of 400 at 40-50 % keystone. A piece removed for changing nothing may have been hidden by a stage in front of it: the dimension from each line came back, worth 20 renders, once the stretched finder was found. After the last change to an order, the parts are measured again and the renders the tests check are chosen again.
- "Nothing lost over every set" is about the sets. A cut that removes a fallback needs the case the fallback exists for, built on purpose. Skipping the full sweep in the regional attempt lost nothing on any set measured, because the sets that turn or offset a symbol were evenly lit and the unevenly lit one was axis-aligned. On the purpose-built case it lost 30 to 47 of each 880. A renderer hides a stage the same way: none drew the top-left finder nearest until the two-axis tilt did, and the first thing that tilt broke was the corner, a stage nobody suspected.
- A regression render must keep needing its mechanism when nudged, and still read around the point. Renders chosen as red before and green after did not tell the centroid from the coverage reading, since either alone read many of them, so each case is chosen with its own mechanism switched off. An exact tie, such as a right-angle turn at a half-pixel offset, tests the rounding and not the geometry. A robustness claim states the grid it was checked on, or checks densely: a 20-nudge search passed renders that failed between its nudges.
- A test asserts its premises both ways: which pass reads the case, that the other attempts fail, and that the strided scan finds nothing. Without those, a later change that reads the case earlier leaves the test green and guarding nothing. When a premise becomes false because the change did its job, the test moves to a case whose premise holds. It is not loosened.
- A bound checked on the test's own symbol is a bound on that symbol. The first failure under a shadow sat two versions from the symbol tested. A reference written from the same description as the code shares its boundaries, so a parity test guards only a boundary its inputs sit on.
- Measure a failure-path gate in the unit its cost is paid in, on the benchmark's own images too. "A grid got past its format information" was rare on the renders a retry was for and true of half of all grids on texture. Completing the stride pass's list cost nothing on one noise generator and doubled the cost on the benchmark's, because the stride pass's early return depends on the texture. Where a fallback sits decides who pays: inside each attempt, the midpoint scan charged every symbol the regional pass reads, and last in the order it charges only the images nothing else reads.
- A fix proposed with a finding is a hypothesis of its own. The regional pass had no negative, and the repair suggested with that finding, inverting the positive's output, read 2 of 48 such renders, where binarizing the negative's own pixels read 44.
- One flag summarizing several measurements is the premise of every rule that reads it. Set by the first failed walk, it stopped describing the sizes measured before that walk. A test case that cannot tell the repair from the defect (crossings on half pixels, equal to the runs, at 0°) is found only by running the defect.
- Read a lead from another reader's code up to the call that gates it. A ring-closure check looked like a detector of its own, but it runs only after four run checks pass, both diagonals at a tolerance this decoder refuses below 2.25 px/module. A lead aimed at renders past the yardstick has to prove itself on real images, or as a check of shipped code.
- Work written from renders of an earlier commit must find them again before it is built. Reading the version through the first transform was written for renders from three changes earlier, and a classification of the failures on the day found none of that kind.
- A check that saves only cost is tested by what the decoder does. Trying other corners without the timing check first changes no result and doubled a damaged symbol's failure time, so a test sees it through a recording stand-in for the steps a corner is tried with.
- A surviving mutant whose substitution never applied looks like dead code. Two survivors of one round were a CRLF file the substitution missed and a pattern whose check matched another line. Re-run after checking that the file changed, one of them was the bound the tests needed most. Mutants and red checks run in a scratch copy of the tree.
- A correct bound can still be the cost. The first like-edge side cap, derived from one distance, was correct but let every column walk a third of the centre past the ratio's own cap, most of a 4 to 5 % read cost. The exact maxima of the conditions, from a small linear program, removed it. Switching one part off at a time found it where timing the whole change could not.
